summary: The Inner Sphere is the oldest settled space there is: twelve inhabited systems, about 85 billion people, and six Builtworld cities among them, all within a few jumps of Sol.
It lives on what it makes and eats: food, alloys, goods and medicine go out, while water, metals, fuel, chemicals and components come in, mostly from the Concord Worlds and the middle ring.
Federation navy yards at Alpha Centauri, Epsilon Eridani, Procyon and Tau Ceti hold it together, and they are now being stripped for ships and crews to feed the Shadow front.
Prism holds 61 Cygni and Struve 2398 A as company towns inside Federation space, with the rest of Prism Incorporate behind them, and nobody here forgets whose cores fly their ships.
The Calder March, which Ironhull crews call the Seam, is six old, crowded systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, where Compact, Federation and Prism space meet.
Ore and metals go inward through Calder's inspections, food goes out from Merrow, water and fuel from Ostry, and medicine and credit from Serein. The debts flow back.
Navigation cores from Quire go inward under escort, so the March's own yards run short while the most valuable cargo around passes through them.
Lanes lead to the Anvil, to Prism's inner systems, and to Varrow and Facet, both under quarantine as glass. Nobody in the March likes to look that way for long.
It has been policed, taxed and argued over for a century and never fought over. The navy is leaving for the Shadow front, and what holds the Seam together is habit.
The Reach is fourteen outer-ring systems, about fourteen million people, strung along lanes of two to three days and every one of them flying the Freeflag colours.
Its ice and gas ports ship water, fuel and chemicals outward, and it lives on imported food, components, medicine and whatever else the smugglers can get past the navy.
Most of it was settled between 2328 and 2406 by ice crews and debtors, then taken over by Freeflag, whose havens turned old ice towns into refit yards.
Four systems, Strike, Last Light, Hope and Remembrance, open towards the Drift, and eighteen dead systems around them make every lane a choke point someone can watch.
Federation patrols are thin, Prism's debts are still owed, and Ironhull crews from the Anvil trade here with more sympathy than the Compact admits.

The Anvil is the Ironhull Compact's heartland: thirty worlds and towns of miners, refiners and forge crews, about four billion people, strung across the middle and outer rings among a lot of dead red dwarfs.
It ships ore, metals, chemicals, alloys and components inward, and lives on imported food, water, fuel, medicine and anything that comes in a box, so every hauler's schedule is a political matter.
The Compact levies are paid to the Federation, but the strikes are remembered here, and Freeflag sympathy runs high along the Reach and Shoals borders, where lanes dip into Freeflag space.
Since 2524 the Anvil has had a hole in its flank: the quarantined Glass systems sit beside Chi Draconis, and the families of Varrow and Hesk still have no answers.
The outer Anvil, from Tarn and Mattock to GJ 3920, opens onto the Drift, which means smugglers, salvagers and Shadow rumours arrive together.
Beacon Cells is a thin pocket of the outer ring: one living system, Dawnward, and four dead ones strung around a blue giant that makes the whole place easy to hide in.
Nearly all of it is Freeflag's, and it trades in what a rebellion needs: quiet berths, patched hulls, fuel, and silence about who was here.
The only way in from the Anvil is the lane out of Onkaria, held by the Ironhull Compact, so the region's one real border runs through a choke point.
Freeflag crews and Ironhull haulers share it more easily than their governments admit, since many Ironhulls remember the strikes and Tarrow.
What it lacks is anything worth a navy's attention, which is why Freeflag chose it.
The Black Shelf is a wide scatter of fifty-nine dead systems one jump past the last human beacons, charted by survey ships and visited mostly by people who cannot afford to be seen.
Nobody settles here: the stars are red dwarfs, white dwarfs and the odd bloated giant, and the planets are either scorched, frozen or not worth the fuel to reach.
What trade there is runs through it rather than to it, with haulers cutting between the Anvil, the Long Dark and the Shoals to dodge navy inspection and Prism's tolls.
Salvagers work the old survey buoys and abandoned claim markers, and the lanes are known mainly for being empty, which suits anyone who wants to vanish or wait.
Blackspace is a thin scatter of Blackhull havens, about eight million people in four settled systems, most of them at Low Tide, with a string of dead red dwarfs in between.
Its one export is water, cut as ice and hauled out by crews who ask little of their buyers; everything else is imported.
Food, fuel, components, goods and medicine all come in from outside, because nothing here grows or gets built, and the ports charge accordingly in favours and silence.
The havens are bound by the Blackhull trade: shared hulls, shared grudges, and a habit of sheltering anyone the Federation or Prism wants to find.
Distance divides them: the settled systems sit days apart behind empty stars, with the Concord Worlds, the Drift, the Shoals and the Far Lanterns all pressing on the edges.
Blightspace is twenty-one systems of dim stars and dead ends beyond Corran Gate, charted by the navy as held by the Shadow since 2519 and settled by nobody.
Nothing is traded here and nobody sails here on business: what the navy knows comes from picket logs and long-range scans, and the rest is guesswork.
Three ways in are known: the lane from emptied Corran into GJ 4074, and two lanes from emptied Mallory, at 44 Ophiuchi and Gl 654.3, with a third into Gl 695.1.
Pulsars, black holes and a red giant make the region hazardous even with the Shadow left out, which is part of why the navy has never tried to retake any of it.
The Cells are five outer-ring systems held by Freeflag, each cut off from the rest of the rebellion and from each other by dead stars, and about eight million people live in them.
They sell water, fuel and chemicals, mostly from ice haulers and gas skimmers, and buy in food, components, goods and medicine through lanes that are short of friends.
Bread alone holds three-quarters of the people; Free Harbor holds most of the rest, and the other three systems together hold only a few thousand more than a large ship's company.
What binds the Cells is Tarrow in 2499 and a shared refusal to let a Federation ship dock; what divides them is distance, thin supply and a long habit of arguing.
The Concord Worlds are the Federation's larder: thirty settled systems and about fifty-seven billion people, most of them in the inner ring and fed from their own fields.
They sell food and manufactured goods and import almost everything else: water, metals, fuel, chemicals, alloys, components and medicine, hauled in largely from Ironhull mines and Prism's houses.
Sixty dead systems lie among the farms: white dwarfs, cold rocks and a red giant that serve as lane junctions, picket stations and, along the borders, hiding places.
Federation law and the navy bind the region, but its edges pull away: Blackhull havens at Low Tide, the Margins, Prism's border at Gl 445, and Freeflag's raids reaching towards Providence.
The Glass and the Shadow have not reached these worlds, but the navy's requisitioned freighters and Prism's core recall are already thinning the shipping that feeds them.
Corran Gate is a chain of five dead systems on the far edge of the outer ring, and nobody lives in any of them now.
Nothing is traded here. Three of the systems were settled by people with little else to try, and the Shadow emptied all three between 2521 and 2523.
The lanes run from The Long Watch through Gl 629.3 and The Metronome to the emptied systems, then out into Blightspace. The Federation holds the near end and has nothing at the far end.
Corran Gate is where the Shadow first came through, so the navy treats it as the front. Everyone further in treats it as somewhere they would rather not go.
The Drift is ninety-odd dead or barely charted systems, mostly red dwarfs and cinders, wedged between nine settled regions and belonging to none of them.
Nobody lives here, so the trade is salvage, smuggled cargo and rumour, carried by crews who want a lane that no customs cutter bothers to watch.
Freeflag boats, Blackhull runners and navy pickets all use the same unmarked lanes, which keeps everyone polite and nobody honest.
Charts of the Drift are thin and out of date, and a captain who buys one should assume the survey was done in a hurry by someone short of fuel.
The Far Lanterns is seventy dead stars strung between the Concord Worlds, Prism Research and the Bloom's Garden and Hedge, with not one settled system among them.
It trades in nothing but transit: salvagers, Blackhull runners and navy pickets use its lanes as back doors between the rings and the Drift.
Its stars are a spread of reds, browns and white dwarfs. Each was surveyed, found wanting and left on the charts, and the lanterns of the name are the dim beacons the survey ships left behind.
Every neighbour wants the lanes open and nobody wants the stars. Prism, the Federation, the Blackhull havens and the Bloom's borders all cross here, and nobody asks who is watching.
The Furnace Deeps is a short, hot chain of three systems: Chara, the one place anyone lives, then a Wolf-Rayet star, then a brown dwarf with nothing on it.
Its only trade is ore and refined metal, which Chara's refineries take from the mining systems of the neighbouring Anvil and ship back out along the same lanes.
The Deeps is Ironhull Compact space throughout, and it runs on Compact habits: levy paid on time, no questions asked of a hull that looks the part.
What divides it is distance: Chara is a crowded town of working people, while the two systems beyond it are empty, dangerous or both, and nobody goes there without a reason.
The Garden is Bloom space: twenty living worlds charted by human surveyors since contact in 2376, set among twenty-one dead systems that nobody has ever settled or been asked to.
Humans come as travellers and surveyors under the Accord, so there are no colonies, no mines and no flags, only survey stations, buoys and the occasional carrier on a licensed run.
What trades here is mostly information and carriage: charts, instrument runs and passage for the few people the Bloom permits, since nothing that grows may be taken.
The rim is where people meet it: Pollen's lane to Wrack in the Anvil, and Zosma, Mossdeep, Rhizome and Seedbed facing the Hedge and the Far Lanterns.
Since Shadowfall the Bloom has closed parts of its sector without explanation, and the Garden is where humans notice it first, in lanes that are quieter and buoys that stay dark.
The Hedge is a tangle of ten living Bloom worlds and seven dead stars, lying between the Garden and the Far Lanterns and charted by human surveyors from 2390 to 2410.
Almost nothing is shipped out of it: humans trade in survey data, lane passage and patience, because under the Accord anything that grows stays where it grows.
The Accord binds every visitor here: no weapons hot near a living world, no cutting or collecting, and no torch burned through a seeding, whatever the schedule says.
Since Shadowfall the Bloom has gone quieter in the Hedge, and surveyors on the Garden side report fewer greetings, shifted lane markers and no explanation offered.
The Ironhull Outposts are two mining systems, Grist and 85 Pegasi, joined by a two-day lane and cut off from the rest of the Compact.
They trade ore, refined metal and forged plate, and most of it goes the long way round to Compact yards, because the short ways run through dead space.
Both lie against The Cells, a run of empty systems, so everything the Outposts own hangs on the two lanes that lead out through Gl 12.
Charter Strike memories and anger over Varrow and Hesk bind the Outposts to the Compact, though distance leaves them feeling forgotten by it.
Lighthouse Run is a short pocket of lanes around a pulsar, where the Federation's inner ring meets the middle ring and the edge of Blackhull space.
New Lagos feeds and garrisons the Federation side, while Barnacle, across the choke point, moves containers for Blackhull crews and asks no questions about what is inside.
Grain, containers and navy stores run one way, and contraband and quiet favours run the other, with both ends of the lane watched by people who know it.
Everything here turns on the Lighthouse, a pulsar nobody can live beside, whose lanes every captain in the Run must cross.
The Long Dark is a hundred-odd systems with nobody living in them, a drift of brown dwarfs, red dwarfs and cold cinders wedged between seven settled regions.
It trades nothing in any ledger, but prospectors, salvagers and smugglers use its empty lanes as back roads between the Concord Worlds, the Margins and the Maw.
Most of its systems carry only survey numbers, because the Rush ran out of money before anyone came back to name them, and the few real names are claims nobody finished.
Every neighbour borders it and none holds it: the navy is too stretched to patrol it, and captains who use it go quietly and keep their fuel high.
Since the Glass took the systems beside Prism Research, crews have been warier of the lanes on that side, and the Long Dark's silence feels less like peace than it used to.
The Long Watch is a string of Federation-held lanes where two crowded, well-fed worlds, Gl 581 and Gamma Pavonis, sit among ten dead stars that nobody has ever made pay.
It trades food and freight: grain and processed agri goods out of the two worlds, and container traffic moving through their ports towards the Concord Worlds and the inner ring.
The navy holds the region, and the dead systems are where its pickets, beacons and inspection stops sit, since every lane here is also a border or a way out to the edge.
Its edges touch the Margins, the Drift, the Outer Dark and Corran Gate, so outside trouble arrives first as a late freighter or a silent picket.
What divides it is plain: the two living worlds are rich and orderly, and everything beyond them is empty, watched and getting closer.
The Margins is a ragged scatter of twenty-four settled systems among forty-nine dead ones, wedged between the Concord Worlds, the Anvil, Prism Research, the Drift and the dark edges beyond.
About 139 million people live here, and nearly 95 million of them are at Vasquez; most other Margins towns are small, thinly guarded and a long way from anyone's help.
It ships water, ore, fuel and chemicals out, and pays dearly for food, components, goods and medicine, which is how Prism's lenders and the navy's inspectors find their way in.
Every settled system here is independent, and nobody agrees what that means: some mean free of the Federation, some mean free of debt, and most just mean nobody has sent a bill yet.
With the Shadow at the far edge and the Glass eating the inner middle ring, the Margins is a back door that may soon be a front line.
Mirrorspace is the spacers' name for the four middle-ring systems that went glass in 2524: Lucerne, Facet, Varrow and Hesk, strung along the borders of the Anvil, the Calder March and the Reach.
It trades nothing, because the Federation shut the lanes in under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine, and no ship sent in has come back.
Two of the four were Prism systems and two were Ironhull mines, so each side has dead of its own and a story it would sooner not tell.

What binds the neighbouring systems is the silence: the Compact's anger at the cover-up, the Federation's closed lanes and Prism's polite recall of certain navigation cores all end at the same four dead lanes.
The Outer Dark is a scatter of sixty-odd dead stars beyond the settled rings: black holes, dwarfs and one tired giant, charted because the lanes run through them, not because anyone wanted them.
Nothing is mined or farmed here, and almost nothing is traded; ships pass through on lanes to the Margins, the Long Watch and the Concord Worlds, or cut across to the Drift when someone is hiding.
What binds it is the lanes: every dead system is a stop between somebody's ports, and the navy, Freeflag raiders and salvagers all use them and trust none of the others.
Since Shadowfall the quiet counts for less, because a dead system with no traffic is where a picket would be posted and where a shade could arrive unseen.
Prism Incorporate is thirteen company worlds packed around the inner ring's edge, home to about seventeen billion people who work for, rent from and owe the same polite landlord.
It ships alloys, components, finished goods and medicine outward, and lives on imported food, water, metals, fuel and chemicals, so every hungry hold in the region is a good one.
Its borders are mostly paperwork: the Inner Sphere to the Sol side, the Concord Worlds and the Ironhull Anvil at choke-point lanes, and the Calder March beyond Gl 625.
The one border nobody has paperwork for is Mirrorspace, where Lucerne went glass in 2524; Prism calls its cores recall precautionary, and everyone nearby counts the lanes anyway.
Wages are good, unrest is low and security is heavy, which holds right up to the day a navigation core is recalled and nobody will say what was wrong with it.
Prism Research is three company systems strung along the outer ring, about 766 million people in all, cut off from the inner ring where the rest of Prism's holdings lie.
Forges, habitats and laboratories turn out alloys, components, goods and medicine, and the region imports nearly everything else: food, water, metals, fuel and chemicals all arrive by hauler.
Four dead systems fill the gaps between the worlds, two of them red-star gateways to the open Drift, and the only lane out toward independent space runs through a red giant.
Prism is landlord, employer and law here, and polite about it. Associates keep their jobs and their company housing, and nobody out here forgets who owns the debt on both.
The Shoals is sixty-odd dead systems with no settlement in any of them: stars with nothing worth the mortgage, strung on lanes that people use only to get somewhere else.
It trades in nothing. What moves through it is Ironhull ore haulers cutting corners, Freeflag runners keeping off navy charts, Blackhull crews going home, and the odd salvager hoping for a wreck.
Its edges are held by people who disagree about everything else: Ironhull mines in the Anvil, Freeflag worlds in the Reach and the Cells, Blackhull havens in Blackspace, and the Drift beyond.
With the navy stretched between Freeflag and the Shadow, nobody patrols the Shoals, so everyone passing through is quietly hoping they are the only ones who thought of it.
The Maw is two dead systems in the Drift, a black hole and a white dwarf, with nobody living in either and no flag claiming them.
Nothing is traded here; the only cargo is whatever surveyors, salvagers and the odd lost captain carry out in their holds and their logs.
Every lane runs back through the Long Dark, and the dwarf also has one lane to the Far Lanterns, so the region is something you cross rather than reach.
What binds the two systems is the same thing that divides them: long, empty jumps of two days or more, and no port, beacon or tug between any of them.
The Sink is a dead-end pocket of the middle ring: one small independent town, Tenpenny, hemmed in by four lifeless stars, one of them a black hole.
Its only export is what Tenpenny can cut or skim: ice from the outer bodies and gas for fuel, sold to anyone desperate or cheap enough to come this way.
Traffic arrives from the Margins by way of Gl 118, or from the Concord Worlds side, and then has to cross the black hole's lane to reach the town.
Nothing binds the region and no flag claims it, which suits Tenpenny and makes it a convenient place to be unrecorded.

bullets: Every jump lane in human space is measured from here, and the torch that scattered people across the Solar System in 2076 is still taught in schools as the day it all began.
One planet has been built over into a single city of about 13 billion, and the habitats, container-port, relay and shipyard keep six lanes busy.
Unrest is low and security is the highest anywhere, but the quarantine of the Glass systems is only ever described here as a hazard notice, and clerks have learned to stop asking.
The shipyard is now receiving navy requisition orders for Ironhull refits, and a captain who knows which hull numbers are on the list could sell that to someone.
Alpha Centauri was settled in 2182, six years after the Valhalla Result, and today an entire planet there has been built over into a city of about 12 billion.
Its military port makes it a fleet base as much as a shipyard town, and half the container traffic out of Sol is sorted here.
The navy has been taking crews from the docks for the Shadow front, and families who no longer hear from their sailors have started gathering at the gates.
Dockhands say the base is pulling in ships faster than the yard can refit them, and a hauler with spare repair crews could name its own terms.
Barnard's Star, a red dwarf, was settled in 2178 as a farm world, and its fields and habitats still grow food for the cities nearer Sol.
With about 836 million people it is the poorest of the inner worlds, and the farmers have a long list of grievances about contract prices.
Water and fuel arrive late and cost more every season, and the unrest here is among the highest in the region, though nobody has so far done more than complain.
A grain broker on the container dock is quietly buying up harvest futures from farmers who fear a requisition, and she needs a ship that doesn't file its manifests.
Wolf 359 was settled in 2184 by agricultural crews, and the red dwarf's dim light still shapes the long, pale-leaved crops the farms are known for.
Its relay and container-port make it the Federation's gate to the Concord Worlds, with lanes running to both Gl 473A and GJ 3622.
Security here is among the heaviest anywhere, with patrols boarding any ship coming in from the Concord side, and the rumour is that they're hunting for smuggled data, not goods.
Inspectors have a habit of losing sealed containers in transit, and a captain with a clean paper trail could find out who benefits.
Sirius was settled in 2176, the year of the Valhalla Result, and its older families still claim to have been first out of Sol on jump drives.
Under its white sun, farms and habitats share the world with a relay that carries traffic from Procyon, Ross 614 and Kapteyn's Star on to Sol.
It is prosperous and orderly, but the relay is crowded with navy signals nobody will explain, and the Concord lanes feel uncomfortably close to the front.
A relay technician has been logging messages that vanish from the queue before they reach Sol, and wants someone to carry the copies out.
Epsilon Eridani was settled in 2186, and a whole planet has since been built over into a city of 13 billion beneath an orange sun.
Its shipyard and military port make it one of the navy's biggest bases, with a lane to Keid in the Concord Worlds for fleet supply.
Yard workers have been told to refit and ready every hull they can for the Shadow front, and the overtime is making them as resentful as it makes them rich.
Some of the ships coming into the yard are Ironhull haulers taken on requisition, and their crews are drinking in the lower docks with plenty to say.
61 Cygni was founded by Halcyon in 2218, and today the whole Builtworld is a Prism holding of about 11 billion people who are employees, tenants or both.
Its forge, research and relay ports make it the sort of place where navigation cores might be made, though Prism has never said which ones.
Since the recall of certain navigation cores, associates here speak very carefully, and the city has gone quiet in the way a workplace does before bad news.
A researcher is said to be looking for a captain with no Prism contracts who can carry a recalled core out of the city without registering it.
Procyon was settled in 2188, and its Builtworld, home to about 13 billion people, grew up around a naval anchorage that never closed.
Its military port and relay make it the Federation's gate toward Luyten's Star, GJ 1111 and the Concord Worlds, and convoys form up here before the long runs.
The navy has been requisitioning civilian ships from the docks for the Shadow front, and the dockside crowds are angrier than the security numbers suggest.
A hauler captain with a requisition notice is selling his berth to anyone who can get him out of the system before the navy collects.
Struve 2398 A was settled by Prism in 2216 and has never been anything else: a world of about 1.5 billion people in company housing under an orange sun.
Its forge, habitat and research ports work for Prism alone, and the lanes lead onward into Prism Incorporate at GJ 1245A and Alsafi.
Since the quarantine and the recall, hiring has been frozen and shifts cut, and workers say supervisors have started leaving certain research wings unlit.
A shift foreman will pay to have a sealed crate of foundry tooling moved off-world before the next audit, and he won't say what's in it.
Epsilon Indi was settled late, in 2241, by farm crews who wanted a world of their own, and it is still the smallest inner world at about 310 million people.
Its agri and container ports feed the Concord lanes toward Lacaille 8760 and Gl 832, and the military port keeps a garrison large for a farm town.
Farmers resent the garrison's grain levies, and unrest is higher than any other inner world except Barnard's Star, with the navy's requisitions making it worse.
The garrison commander is quietly selling off surplus fuel to anyone who won't ask where it came from, and a trader could make friends or enemies with that.
Tau Ceti was settled in 2194, and a planet there has been built over into a single city of about 14 billion, the largest in human space.
Its shipyard and military port are among the busiest anywhere, with lanes to Gl 54.1, Gl 65A and Epsilon Eridani all within two days.
Everything here is rich and secure on the surface, but the yard is running three shifts on Shadow-front refits, and the strain shows in the lower decks.
Yard inspectors have been finding hulls with nav cores that don't match their records, and a captain with a Prism receipt might learn why.
HIP 82724 was settled in 2204 as a farm and freight world, and today about 3.9 billion people live under its yellow sun.
Its agri, container and relay ports serve five lanes, four of them into the Concord Worlds and one back to Alpha Centauri, making it a busy crossroads.
Prosperous and tightly policed, it nonetheless sees too much traffic from the Concord side for the harbourmasters to inspect, and the backlog grows each week.
A harbourmaster's clerk is selling clearance slots to captains who can pay in kind, and sooner or later somebody in uniform will notice.
Groombridge 34 is a red dwarf with nobody living there; Prism holds it for its position, a lane junction between Ross 248 and Achird in Prism Incorporate.
It also has a lane to The Lighthouse across the border into Lighthouse Run, which makes this dead system a choke point that Prism would rather keep quiet.
Ice crews of the belt tradition settled Ostry in 2282, cutting towns into an ice moon because a red dwarf gave them nothing warmer.
Ostry sells water and fuel to the whole March and buys everything else. Most of its 150 million people live under the ice and know each other's families.
Its people are closer to the Blackhulls than the Compact admits, and a Blackhull hull in the tug yards draws a shrug rather than a report.
Most of the people who got out of Varrow came through here, and the quarantine picket at the jump zone is watched like a dog that has bitten someone.
Plenty of Varrow's crews left debts, kin and unanswered questions behind, and a captain who carries a message across the picket would find buyers under the ice.
Halcyon Dynamics terraformed Serein from 2301 as a company world, and it is still Prism's seat in the March: white towers, managed gardens, orbital clinics.
Its 2.8 billion people are associates, their families and the staff who serve them. Everything is clean, quiet and expensive, and the politeness has an edge.
Prism's statement on the 2524 quarantine was issued here, and every associate repeats it word for word, down to the pauses.
Serein holds the debts of half the Ironhull crews in the March, and since Varrow fell some of those debtors cannot be found, though the ledgers stay open.
The research ports are busy while the recall of navigation cores goes on. A captain who is asked to carry a sealed case to Serein should ask what is in it, and expect no answer.
Halcyon built the first foundries on Quire's scorched inner world in 2284, and worker domes and orbital habitats grew up on the night side to serve them.
Quire forges navigation cores, the most valuable cargo in the March, and its relay port sends them inward under heavy guard rather than to the local yards.
Quire was sister plant to the foundry that went glass in 2524. Output is down, and staff on fixed contracts are rotated out faster than anyone explains.
Its 600 million people are quiet because they have contracts to keep. Rotated-out staff talk freely in Merrow's bars about what the sister plant was making before it went silent.
Farmers and a Federation charter settled Merrow in 2294 to feed the mining systems, and it is still the only world in the March where food grows in the open.
About 7.5 billion people live here, nearly half the March, in farm towns, processing cities and container ports that ship food to everyone, Ironhull and Prism alike.
Merrow is comfortable and a little smug, but the war levy has gone up twice and evacuees from the Shadow front are filling its towns faster than it can house them.
The lane to Facet, a system gone glass, is only 1.7 days away. Merrow's navy base is cut off from the Federation core, and farmers who watch the lane are not reassured.
Evacuees and locals are competing for harvest work and housing, and a captain hauling relief cargo might find who gets it a bigger fight than the hauling.
The navy settled Calder in 2292 as a base to watch the Seam, and the cities on its thin-aired, dry world grew up round the station like moss round a post.
Calder Station holds the picket squadron, customs and the Compact's levy office, and every Ironhull cargo going inward passes through its inspections.
The navy is being pulled to the Shadow front, and the junior officers left behind are overworked, touchy and inclined to find something wrong with any hold.
Calder's lane to Varrow is closed as glass, and the picket crews who supply the Ostry quarantine talk freely in the station's bars about what they have been told not to say.
Mining crews settled Brannock in 2293 under company charters, working the scorched world Cinder and gas giant Vast, and Halde's arcologies later took in the March's biggest crowd.
It is the Ironhulls' hub in the March: ore from Cinder, metals from Tallow's refinery, hulls from Kettle Yard, all sent inward under the Federation's inspectors, whom Brannock resents.
Blackhulls drink in its docks and the dock police look elsewhere, in the way a family treats a cousin who is in trouble.
Some two million Varrow crew and kin now live on Halde in emptied towers and borrowed habs, angry about the cover-up and unsure whom to blame for it.
Kettle Yard has navy orders to refit haulers for the front and is slow to fill them. Yard hands will quietly fit guns for the right captain and the wrong flag.
Alshain was set up in 2365 as an outwatch, a handful of crews holding a beacon and a watch post on the lane to the dead orange star Gl 735.
Two thousand people now live here, and the haven is the only thing of value: a place where raiders can patch hulls without being asked what for.
Security is close to nothing and unrest runs high, since the Freeflag flags went up and the Federation stopped sending anything but warnings.
Ships keep arriving from Gl 735 with their transponders dark, which should be impossible for a system with nobody in it, and the watchers are not agreed on who they are.
Standfast was settled in 2328 around 18 Scorpii, when the Rush still paid for ice and nobody expected the contracts to run out.
The name dates from when the first contract failed and the colonists voted to stay and keep digging, which is why it later made an easy Freeflag town.
About 123 thousand people live here, cutting water from the ice and patching Freeflag converted freighters in the haven berths.
Three of its four lanes lead into dead systems, so every arrival from there is either salvage or trouble and is treated as both.
A runner out of GJ 3937, whose red giant is a poor place to hide, is said to have come back with cargo nobody will name.
Openhand began as an ice town in 2338 on a promise of no questions asked, and four million people have since taken it at its word.
Its ice moves down the lanes to Standfast and Reckoning, and the haven turns away nobody with a hull to repair and a reason to leave.
Unrest is among the highest in the Reach because the town is crowded, the medicine runs short, and the Federation notices it more than the smaller colonies.
Captains running medicine here are not asked where they got it, only how much, and the clinic queues are what settle the answer.
Mutual was settled in 2371 by an ice co-operative, and its founding charter, still pinned up in the dock office, makes every worker a part-owner of the hull.
About 137 thousand people live here, running ice and the haven berths on shared accounts that Freeflag command has found very convenient.
Security is among the lowest in the Reach and unrest the highest, since the co-op wants a vote and Freeflag wants ice delivered.
The lane to Gl 735 is a choke point both Mutual and Alshain watch, and the co-op watch crews do not agree on what they have seen come through it.
Shoulder, settled in 2353 around Tau Boötis, takes its name from the way the three lanes into it seem to lean on the one into Footwall.
About 234 thousand people cut ice and keep a haven, and the town does well enough that its unrest sounds like grievance more than hunger.
Freeflag treats it as a working crossroads, with the Drift lane to the dead system GJ 3790 the only one that ever gets quiet.
Ships leave for Footwall, a dead system Freeflag nonetheless holds, and come back with their holds sealed and their crews saying very little.
Two Hundred was settled in 2348 as a gas-scooping town at 99 Herculis, and took its present name after Tarrow, in 2499, for the people vented there.
Three million people scoop fuel here and run a haven, and the fuel feeds most of the converted freighters in the north of the Reach.
Security is thin and unrest high, and the town has never forgiven the navy for Tarrow, so Federation ships are not served here at any price.
A lane runs to Dawnward in the Beacon Cells, and the fuel convoys that take it travel with armed escorts nobody has ever seen paid.
Reckoning is an outwatch of about a thousand people, put on the lane to Vug Reach in 2356 to keep an eye on a brown dwarf nobody can settle.
It cuts ice and has no haven, which suits it, as the quiet gives the few crews who pass through somewhere to be unobserved.
Unrest is very high for so small a place, because everyone there is a debtor or a deserter and the nearest help is three days off.
A ship that comes in from Vug Reach, where nobody lives, is welcomed with caution, and the watch crews keep a log of each one.
Common was settled in 2358 as a shared outpost at 59 Virginis, where the founders pooled their claims and called the pool the common.
About eight thousand people live here, and its single haven keeps the outpost supplied by repairing Freeflag raiders and asking for food in return.
Unrest is very high and security low, since the outpost is too small to defend and too useful to be left alone.
The lane to GJ 1172 leads into the dead Drift, and people say supplies come and go that way at night, with nobody willing to say whose.
Kinship, settled in 2375 at 15 Sagittae, was founded by ice-crew families who had followed each other out from the same dying belt station.
About four thousand people live here and cut ice for Last Light and Mutual, in a place where nearly everyone is related and not always happily.
Security is low and the lane to dead Kettle is a choke point with nothing to watch it but the families themselves.
Two more dead systems lie behind Kettle, and the families disagree about whether the ships they sometimes see out there are salvagers, ghosts or a mistake.
Diadem was settled in 2361 as a gas town, where the first scoops hung over the giant like a ring of lights and gave the place its name.
Two million people now scoop fuel and keep a haven, and the fuel is a large part of what keeps Freeflag hulls moving.
Unrest is high but the town is not poor, and what it resents is the Federation's habit of calling its fuel contraband.
The lane to the dead Drift system GJ 3790 is rarely used, and a few fuel haulers swear that someone keeps it clear all the same.
Strike was settled in 2372 and renamed after the Charter Strikes, when ice crews from the middle ring came through with nowhere to go and stayed.
About 31 thousand people live here, running ice and a haven, and it is the Reach's main door into the open Drift.
Security is the lowest in the Reach, because the lane to Tarn leads straight to the Ironhull Compact and the Compact's crews are welcome.
Compact crews from Tarn bring news of Varrow and Hesk and the families who were told nothing, and Strike is where that anger gets turned into Freeflag recruits.
Last Light was settled in 2406, long after the Rush ran out of money, by crews who had lost everything in the strikes and were running short of places to try.
About four million people live here and cut ice and keep a haven, and it is the largest of the Reach's Drift gateways.
Unrest is high, because most of its families were driven out of somewhere, and few of them are inclined to trust a Federation ship or a Prism ledger.
Ships come in from HIP 97051, a dead Shoals system, without registry or cargo manifests, and Last Light asks no more about them than it does about anyone else.
Hope was settled in 2391, in the middle of the Charter Strikes, by a crew who called their ice claim Hope because it was the only cheerful word on the filing form.
About 326 thousand people cut ice and keep a haven, which makes Hope a larger place than its name or its security would suggest.
Unrest is among the highest in the Reach, since Hope is a way out towards the Drift and every Federation ship that stops there has an opinion on it.
The lane to HIP 90265 leads into a dead Shoals system, and it is said that Freeflag keeps a supply cache there that it would rather the Federation did not find.
Remembrance was settled in 2374 as an outpost at 45 Boötis, and its name came from the list of dead crew painted on the first dock wall.
About seven thousand people live here, and the single haven serves ships passing between Strike and the dead Shoals system GJ 3853.
Security is thin and unrest very high, and the outpost keeps its list of names up to date, which now includes people killed by the Federation.
Captains passing through are asked to add a name, and a few say the wall has started to include names of people who are not dead yet.
Gl 735 is an orange star in the middle ring that nobody has settled, and its only lanes lead to Alshain and Mutual, two Freeflag systems that watch it.
Nobody is meant to live there, and the two systems that border it disagree on what has been coming out of it.
Footwall is a yellow star with no settlement, yet Freeflag holds it, and it sits on the lane between Shoulder and the Ironhull system Arcturus.
Nobody lives there, but Shoulder's ships go in empty and come out sealed, so it is plainly being used for something.
Sharjah is a red dwarf, flare-prone and dim, and nobody has lived there because the star punishes habitats and offers little ice in return.
The only useful lane runs to Standfast, so the system sees traffic only from salvagers and from crews who have a reason to be out of sight.
Kettle is an orange star with no settlement, and it sits at the end of Kinship's lane, a choke point that leads on to two more dead systems.
Nobody lives there, but the short lanes to Gl 777A and HIP 101516 make it a handy place to lie quiet, and a few ships do.
GJ 3937 is a red giant, swollen and unstable, and it is the Reach's real hazard, with radiation and heat that kill any habitat built near it.
Its only useful lane leads to Standfast, and Standfast's crews keep it as a choke point that nobody has ever been tempted to cross.
Vug Reach is a brown dwarf, too dim to warm a habitat and too far from anything to be worth an ice claim, so nobody lives there.
Its lane to Reckoning is a choke point, and Reckoning's watch crews log every ship that comes out of it, because very few have a reason to go in.
Chi Draconis was settled in 2257 by ore-prospectors from Sol who found the belts rich and the sun dependable, and it has been a Compact town since the Charter Strikes.
Its nineteen million people work a mine and a refinery, and ore from the outer Anvil often passes through here on its way inward.
Lucerne, one lane away at under two days, went glass in 2524, and the quarantine buoys now sit in sight of Chi Draconis traffic.
Unrest is above the Anvil's average: dock crews talk openly about the cover-up, and the navy inspectors have stopped enjoying their visits.
A captain willing to carry unofficial letters from relatives of Lucerne's lost crews could find a lot of grateful, angry people at the refinery bars.
Swarf was settled in 2279 around 61 Virginis, and grew into a forge world of some two hundred million on the back of cheap ore and stubborn labour.
It mines, refines and forges, and its sheet and structural alloys are shipped to half the Compact.
Two of its three lanes lead to dead red dwarfs, so everything comes and goes by a single busy route through GJ 3707.
Swarf is calmer than most of the Anvil, but its yards are full of haulers being fitted with guns, and the foremen are quietly arguing about who they are really for.
Stour, around Beta Comae Berenices, was settled in 2286 by a mining co-operative that never quite stopped being one.
Twenty-one million people mine and refine here, and the town is steady, orderly and proud of its low unrest.
Its lane to Chara links the Anvil to the Furnace Deeps, so Stour's docks see a lot of Deeps metal on the way somewhere else.
A refinery shift that has lost its foreman to a navy requisition is said to be looking for a replacement who is not too fond of paperwork.
61 Ursae Majoris was settled in 2277 and stayed a quiet mining town, a few strikes and one memorable flood of coolant its only notable history.
Seventeen million people work its mine and refinery, and the town sends refined stock to Alula Australis and Chara by short lanes.
It is a secure, well-run place by Anvil standards, and its harbour authority is known for fining everyone equally.
Crews complain that the navy's requisition lists have taken three tugs without paying, and a captain with a spare hull might find work.
Quarle was settled in 2254 around an orange sun, among the earliest of the Anvil's worlds, and now holds some 137 million people.
It mines, refines and forges, and it is the Compact's front door to Prism's Gl 643, whose customs sit across a choke point.
Prism pays well and asks politely, which makes Quarle's forge masters suspicious, and the recall of navigation cores has not helped.
Gl 654, the dead system on the other lane, is a favourite stop for ships who would rather not be logged at Quarle's docks.
Pollux was settled in 2304 around a swollen red giant, whose bright, wide star makes shipping into the system slow and mining cheap.
Twenty-five million people live in a mining and refining town at the end of a long chain of jumps, ten from Sol.
Its lanes run to GJ 2069A, to a dead system and across a border to a dead Margins star, so very little passes through it by chance.
Pollux has been lonely long enough to resent everyone, and its dockmasters will ask a stranger twice who sent them.
Alula Australis was settled in 2283 by crews from 61 Ursae Majoris who wanted a mine nobody else could tax.
Thirty-one million people mine and refine here, and it is a crossroads town, with lanes to Noquisi, Vug, 61 Ursae Majoris and a dead red dwarf.
It is among the poorer places in the middle ring, and its unrest runs a little above its neighbours' as lanes to the glass cluster grow quieter.
The dead lane to GJ 3667 is an open invitation to salvagers, and the harbour office would rather not know who goes.
Burr, around Iota Persei, was settled in 2285 and grew into a world of over a hundred million, a mining and forge centre of the middle ring.
Its foundries turn out hull plate and drive casings, and Burr lacks only the money to buy back the ore it smelts.
One lane goes to GJ 3126, a dead system on Prism's side of the border, and Prism patrols watch it with interest.
Burr's forge crews have been refitting haulers with guns for months, and the yard foremen remember who burned the strikes' last barricades.
Callow was settled in 2307 and, with ice as well as ore, grew into the Anvil's biggest world, home to about one and a half billion people.
It mines, supplies ice and refines, which makes it a water exporter in a region that mostly begs for it.
With its size comes unrest: the crowded lower decks have been angry since the Glass, and the Compact's police have been stretched thin.
Gl 67, the dead system near Callow and Titawin, is a handy place for hauliers to meet without anyone asking.
Zavijava was settled in 2268, and its three ports mine ore, cut ice and run forges for a population of some four hundred million.
It is a well-fed, prosperous and well-defended Anvil world, and it sends water and alloys to Denebola and Porrima by short lanes.
Security is comparatively high, and the Compact has quietly made Zavijava its main depot for requisitioned hull repairs.
The forge guilds have begun asking who is being protected, and a captain who knows the answer might trade it.
Denebola was settled in 2265 as a small mining colony under a white star, and it has never grown past half a million people.
Its mining and refinery crews are tough and tightly bound, partly because the dead GJ 3667 sits across a choke point just beyond them.
Denebola's position next to GJ 3667, where the quarantine and the glass are said to creep close, makes its folk unwilling to say much.
A lone survey beacon at the edge of its system has been reporting oddities, and nobody at the colony wants to be the one to file it.
Gamma Serpentis was settled in 2291, an ordinary mining town with a refinery and seventeen million people who think of themselves as ordinary.
It sits in a tidy triangle with Gl 609 and Brack, and tends to trade ore and plate with both.
Unrest is middling and rising, mostly over the requisitions and the lack of news from the east.
The harbourmaster keeps a quiet ledger of ships that did not return from navy charters, and has begun to share it with captains he trusts.
Arcturus was settled in 2264 around a red giant, and its forge crews live under a huge, dim, cold-looking sun.
Five million people mine and forge here, a small town with a long memory and a strong sense of its own worth.
One lane runs to Footwall, a Freeflag system, and Freeflag runners sometimes use it, a fact the Compact pretends not to see.
Drift Mouth next door is dead and a good place to meet, and a captain with Freeflag cargo might find a fence in Arcturus.
Cadge, around 11 Leonis Minoris, was settled in 2296, and its mining and forge ports are known for good steel and bad tempers.
Twenty-six million people live in a town that is secure by Anvil standards, with a navy post and an Ironhull yard side by side.
It trades by lane with Copernicus, Wrack and Gant, and its forge masters are among the loudest voices in the Compact's meetings.
Unrest is middling, and a captain hauling guns for the Compact's refit programme could get plenty of work here and plenty of questions.
Porrima was settled in 2290 under a white star, and three million people mine and refine here in the quiet, tidy way of a small and careful town.
It is linked to Zavijava and GJ 3728B, and the red giant system next door gives it a spectacular sky.
Unrest is the lowest on the Anvil, partly because its people have the sense to live quietly.
The lane to Gl 480, a dead system, is rarely used, and the harbour office suspects someone is using it all the same.
Brack was settled in 2315 around Lambda Serpentis, and its fifty million people mine and refine ore for the neighbouring towns.
It is a reliable, workmanlike town, with lanes to Gamma Serpentis, Gl 609 and the more distant GJ 3981.
Its refinery has been running double shifts since the navy began buying alloy, and the extra work has not made anyone happier.
Old hands say the freight clerks at Brack will bend a manifest for a friend, which is useful to a captain who has friends.
Copernicus was settled in 2302, and its thirty million people mine and refine ore in a town known for its sensible dockside.
Lanes run to GJ 2069A, Cadge and Gl 353, which makes it a useful relay for ore moving between the western towns.
Security is middling and unrest low, and the town has been careful to stay out of the quarrels of its bigger neighbours.
A workers' council there is said to be collecting names of crews lost to navy requisition, and wants a courier to carry the list to the Compact.
Hob, around 44 Boötis, was settled in 2297 and became a world of nearly two hundred million, with mines, refineries and a good forge.
Its yards build hauler hulls for the Compact, and the gun mounts now bolted to them are the town's current pride and worry.
Hob is stable and well fed, but its trade lanes lead outward to Skerry, GJ 3873 and Tholl, which are all closer to the Drift than anyone likes.
The yard unions say the navy's requisition lists name Hob ships first, and a captain can hear the grumbling in any bar.
36 Ursae Majoris was settled in 2313 and grew into a world of two hundred million, with mines, refineries and a forge that has outlasted three owners.
It sits between Gant and the outer towns of Chalawan and Clinker, and much of the western ore trade passes through its docks.
Security is fairly good, but the world feels the strain of the outer Anvil's unrest, which flows inward along the lanes.
A forge-master has been quietly buying scrap hulls and paying in cash, which makes some people ask what she is building.
Gant was settled in 2299 around Theta Ursae Majoris, and now holds some three hundred million people on a world the Compact calls outer ring.
Its mines, refineries and forge supply a third of the ore the western Anvil sells, and it knows it.
Security is low and unrest high, and Freeflag pamphlets are found in the dock lockers more often than the harbour police admit.
A captain willing to carry a message between the forge stewards and a Freeflag contact could earn a great deal of trust or a great deal of trouble.
Titawin was settled in 2312 and is a mining, refining and forge world of about 138 million, on the edge of the Compact.
It faces dead systems on two of its three lanes, Gl 67 and Gl 14, so its only living neighbour is Callow.
Security is low, with the navy thin on the ground, and Titawin's people have learned to keep their own watch.
Gl 67 is barely over a day away, and people say salvagers and smugglers meet there beyond the reach of anyone's customs.
Chalawan was settled in 2298 and has become a world of nearly two hundred million, with mines, refineries and forge yards beyond the middle ring.
Its short lane to Vug connects it to Alula Australis, and most of its trade goes that way.
Security is poor, unrest is high, and the Compact has sent little help because it has little to send.
Rumour says a Blackhull crew has been drinking at a dockside bar there, and the harbourmaster has been told not to look.
Holt, around 26 Draconis, was settled in 2305 and holds seventy-five million people who mine and refine in the shadow of the Anvil itself.
It is linked by short lanes to Anvil, Gl 675 and Gl 630.1A, a tight cluster that trades mostly with itself.
Security is thin and unrest close to boiling, with wages fixed at what the Compact can afford and prices fixed at what Prism can charge.
A wildcat strike committee is said to meet in the old ore sheds, and a captain who moves cargo might be asked to carry more than cargo.
Clinker, around Pi-1 Ursae Majoris, was settled in 2321, a late and marginal Anvil town that has never quite stopped being a camp.
Forty-three million people mine and forge here, in a place with little security and a lot of salvage to defend.
Tailings, a dead brown dwarf, lies across a border lane from Clinker, and the town's scrap haulers go there for what they can find.
The town runs on makeshift deals, and a captain who offers honest prices may find it surprising enough to be remembered.
Skerry, around Theta Boötis, was settled in 2310 and has thirty-two million people mining and refining on the edge of the Furnace Deeps.
Its lane to Adit connects it to the Deeps, and Deeps smelters are the town's best customers.
Security is thin, unrest moderate, and the harbour is as crowded with traffic as it is short of patrols.
A rumour of cheap Deeps alloys falling off a hauler has drawn buyers to Skerry, and the harbour police are watching the quay.
Wrack, around 20 Leonis Minoris, was settled in 2318 on the Anvil's border with the Garden, and its fifty-nine million people mine and refine ore.
Its lane to Pollen, a living Bloom world, makes it the Anvil's closest neighbour to something human beings do not understand.
Security is poor and unrest is among the highest on the Anvil, as the Bloom's closed sectors have unsettled traders and navy alike.
The Accord forbids weapons near Pollen, and a captain hauling guns for the Compact's refits had better know which side of that line the cargo sits.
Anvil, around 19 Draconis, was settled in 2330, a small mining and refining town that gave its name to the region long before it grew into one.
Seven million people live there, in a place that feels like a museum of its own pride.
Security is thin, and the town leans on Holt and its neighbouring systems for defence.
People say the original charter is kept in a locked case in the harbour office, and that nobody agrees on what it entitles them to.
Tholl, around Chi Herculis, was settled in 2320, and its mines, ice shipping and forges now support about 122 million people.
It exports water, which in the outer Anvil makes it a kind of banker, and it is hated and courted accordingly.
Security is thin, and the road to the Drift via GJ 3920 and Tarn is only lightly watched.
A captain who can move water quietly past the navy to Freeflag buyers would find Tholl's ice-brokers more than willing to deal.
Tarn, around Rho Coronae Borealis, was settled in 2331 as a late mining and forge town on the very edge of the Compact.
Fifty-nine million people live there, and it is a gateway into the open Drift, with a lane to Strike, a Freeflag system, two days away.
Security is poor and unrest high, with Freeflag sympathy open and navy visits met with closed shutters.
A captain who knows the Drift could be hired here to guide shipments through the unmarked reaches, and to keep quiet about what is carried.
Mattock, around 10 Canum Venaticorum, was settled in 2349, the youngest world in the Anvil, and now has some 104 million people.
It mines, refines and forges, and is a gateway into the open Drift, with a dead Shoals star three days away.
Security is poor and unrest high, as the Compact's levy sits heavy on a world that has had little time to grow.
Salvagers come in from the Drift with strange cargo, and Mattock's yards have a sideline in not asking where it came from.
GJ 1221 is a dead red dwarf on the Compact's books, a faint inner-ring star that nobody has settled, though a Compact beacon marks the lane.
It sits between Chi Draconis and Prism's Gl 445, and its main use is as a place for ships to wait out inspections.
Gl 518 is a dead red dwarf with nothing to mine and no one to claim it, and the Compact has never bothered to fortify it.
Its lanes run to Gar and Gl 536, both dead, and to Swarf, so the only traffic is the occasional Swarf prospector checking old claims.
GJ 3839 is a dead red dwarf held by the Compact, kept as a lane relay, with no population and no reason to have one.
It lies on the lane between Stour and Arcturus and also touches the Federation's Xi Boötis, which makes it a quiet border crossing for the careful.
GJ 3667 is a dead red dwarf with no settlement, flaring now and then, and uneasy rumour says the lanes near it have been behaving oddly.
It joins Denebola and Alula Australis to the Concord Worlds and the Garden, and the Compact has no wish to explain why traffic has thinned.
Gl 433 is a dead red dwarf, a bare system of rock and flares with nothing worth hauling out of it.
Its single quick lane to Gl 432A makes it a dead-end pair, popular with prospectors and with anyone who wants to be left alone.
GJ 3707 is a dead orange star held by the Compact, a lane junction with a beacon but no settlement.
All of Swarf's ore leaves through it, so it is better watched than most dead systems, and the harbour office there keeps a log of its traffic.
Gl 432A is a dead red dwarf, with no known resources and no one in residence beyond whatever the old charts still list.
It is a short hop from Gl 433 and a long one from GJ 3707, so it sees almost nobody.
GJ 3804 is a dead white star near Swarf, bright enough to be pretty and barren enough to be left alone.
Swarf's prospectors have surveyed it more than once and found nothing to mine, and its lane to Gl 536 leads only into more dead space.
Gl 654 is a dead red dwarf with a nearly useless set of rocks, and the Compact only keeps a beacon at its Quarle lane.
Its far lane runs three days to Standfast, a Freeflag system, so it is quietly used by those who know the way.
GJ 3728B is a dead red giant held by the Compact, too bright and too hot for anyone to settle near.
It is a useful junction, with lanes to Porrima, Zavijava, GJ 3707 and Stope, and its radiation keeps ships from loitering.
Gl 67 is a dead red dwarf with no inhabitants, wedged between Titawin and Callow, and unwatched by either of them.
Its short lane to Titawin makes it a convenient meeting place for those who would rather not use a port.
Drift Mouth is a dead red dwarf at the Anvil's outer edge, named for what lies beyond it and unsettled for the same reason.
It connects Arcturus to Gl 480, and its traffic is mostly smugglers who know there is no navy picket.
Gl 164 is a dead white dwarf held by the Compact, a cold, faint remnant with nothing to mine and a beacon to mark the lane.
It links Burr to Capella in the Margins, so the little traffic that passes through is usually independent and discreet.
GJ 3423 is a dead red dwarf, with no known resources and no settlers, sitting on a long border lane from Pollux.
It leads to Pell's Folly in the Margins, and the few who use it are generally avoiding something.
Stope is a dead white dwarf, once surveyed for ore and abandoned when the survey came back empty.
Its lanes lead only to GJ 3728B and GJ 3655, another dead system, so it is more of a dead end than a crossing.
Gl 480 is a dead red dwarf, with no mine and no settlement, notable only for its place among a cluster of empty systems.
Lanes run to Porrima, GJ 3782B and Drift Mouth, and the Porrima harbour office suspects it of being a smugglers' waypoint.
Tailings is a dead brown dwarf, a dim, cold star whose name comes from the scrap that Clinker's crews have hauled out of its orbit.
One lane runs to Clinker and one to Gl 322 in the Cells, three days away, so most visitors are scavengers.
Gl 14 is a dead red dwarf, a faint star with nothing to claim, and it is the last stop before the emptier dead systems beyond.
Its lane to Titawin is long, and the lane to GJ 4381, another dead system, is shorter, so salvagers tend to loop through it.
Gl 649.1A is a dead red dwarf, a day from its twin Gl 651, and the two form a pair of empty systems that few care about.
Its only other lane leads to GJ 3920, nearly three days away, so the pair is as isolated as the charts can make it.
Gl 651 is a dead orange star, a day from Gl 649.1A, and it has never been settled, though some rocks there are said to be worth a look.
Its only other lane leads to GJ 3920, and prospectors who go out to it report mostly emptiness.
GJ 3920 is a dead red dwarf held by the Compact, a gateway into the open Drift, with a beacon and no inhabitants.
Lanes run to Winze Reach, Tholl, the twin dead stars and a dead Shoals system, so it sees smugglers, prospectors and the odd navy picket.
Dawnward was settled in 2334 as an outwatch, a lane-watch post built when the Rush was still paying for such things, with a few hundred crew and not much else.
The money dried up in the 2370s and the post stayed, so its two thousand people are the children of watchkeepers, now keeping watch for Freeflag.
Its one port is a haven, and it asks few questions: converted freighters under painted flags lay up here, patch their hulls and leave before the tide of rumour turns.
Unrest runs high and security low, since no Federation ship has been welcome here since Tarrow, and every captain knows how that ended for the habitat and its two hundred dead.
A captain can find work here carrying parts or messages across the Onkaria choke point, where Ironhull pickets are inclined to look away but the navy's inspectors are not.
Onkaria is a red dwarf with nothing worth settling, no ice worth hauling and no one living there, and the charts keep it only because of where its lanes go.
The Ironhull Compact holds it for the choke point alone: one lane into Freeflag's Beacon Cells, watched by a picket that tallies traffic and, for a modest consideration, mislays some of it.
The Beacon is a blue giant whose radiation scours every rock around it, so nobody lives here and nothing would survive trying.
Freeflag holds it because four lanes meet here and no navy captain wants to sit long in that glare, so convoys cross it quickly and sensors there are mostly noise.
GJ 4029 is a white dwarf with a few dead rocks around it, nothing to mine and nowhere to build, and it was never settled.
Freeflag crews use it as a waypoint on the road to the Reach, where a ship can drift unseen between jumps and wait for the all-clear.
GJ 3972 is a red dwarf at the end of a thin lane, with no settlement and no reason to build one.
Freeflag holds it for the dead end's sake: hulls too damaged for Dawnward's yards are said to be laid up here, stripped for parts and left to cool.
Gl 30 is a red dwarf with a few cold rocks and no one on them; surveyors logged it as a flare risk and moved on.
Its four lanes all lead deeper into the Shelf, which makes it a quiet crossroads for captains who would rather not meet a patrol.
GJ 1034 is a red giant whose swollen star has swallowed or stripped any inner worlds, and its radiation and deep gravity well make loitering a poor idea.
It sits on the lane to the Long Dark, and salvagers say a few survey buoys still ping out there, if you are willing to fly close enough to hear them.
Gl 59.1 is a white dwarf, a dim cooling cinder with nothing left worth building on, which is why the charts carry a survey stamp and no settlement.
Four lanes meet here, and crews crossing the Shelf use it as a dark waypoint, trusting that no one else has a reason to be there.
HIP 3876 is a white dwarf with a faint debris belt and no world fit for anyone, so nobody has ever filed a claim worth keeping.
Hauliers crossing between Gl 59.1 and the deeper Shelf pass through it, and some leave caches here, so a patient scavenger might find one not yet collected.
GJ 3122 is a red dwarf with a few airless rocks and flares frequent enough to make a hab roof a poor investment, so it stayed empty.
The lanes out run to a handful of uncharted Drift systems, and surveyors have never fully mapped what lies at the far ends.
Gl 29.1 is a white dwarf with nothing in orbit but dust and ice, and no one has ever found a reason to stay.
It is the Shelf's far side from the Anvil's traffic, so anyone running dark between Gl 30 and the deeper Drift tends to come through here.
Ice miners settled Low Tide in 2287, long before anyone said Blackhull, and for a century it was a cold, ordinary town shipping water to its neighbours.
After the Charter Strikes, crews who had lost everything drifted in, and the town turned haven; it is now the biggest place in Blackspace, with about six million people.
It is known for ice, and for docks where nobody checks a manifest too closely, with lanes running to Barnacle and across the border to Gl 908 and Van Maanen's Star.
Those two Federation lanes are choke points, and the navy watches them with ships it can ill spare, so inspections and requisition notices are the talk of every bar.
Security is poor and unrest runs high, with Freeflag recruiters working the docks and Ironhull cousins angry about the Glass cover-up, so the town is one bad inspection from a riot.
A hauler captain at the ice docks says the navy is counting hulls at Gl 908 for requisition, and wants a quiet passage out through Barnacle first.
Ice crews settled Deneb Algedi in 2319 under a white sun, in the middle ring, and later the Blackhulls made it a haven.
Every lane out leads to a dead system, so nobody arrives here by accident and ships that do arrive have usually chosen it.
About a million people live here, selling ice and a safe berth, and buying in all the food and medicine they can pay for.
Security is thin and unrest is high, because supplies come the long way round and the Federation's levy collectors have started asking why Blackhulls keep turning up here.
Ironhull relatives have come asking Blackhull crews what they have seen on the quarantined lanes, and a captain who can carry letters and keep quiet will find work.
Blind Eye was settled in 2396, just after the Charter Strikes, by crews with no charter and no home, who gave the place a name that says nobody is watching.
It is a colony of about six hundred and sixty thousand, with an ice port and a haven port, and little else to recommend it.
Security is almost nil, and unrest is high: crews settle quarrels by hand, and Freeflag recruiters find the young easy to talk to.
Two dead red dwarfs lie close behind it, and a long lane runs out to GJ 3505 in the Far Lanterns, towards the edge where the Shadow is.
A hauler is overdue from GJ 3505, and her owners will cut a share to anyone who goes and looks.
Wreckers was settled in 2438 as an outwatch, a few hundred salvagers working the hulks in the red dwarf systems behind it, and it still has one haven port.
About two thousand people live here, with no ice, no farms and no law, so every meal and every part is imported.
Security is almost nonexistent and unrest is high, because the salvage has thinned and the hungry crews have started eyeing one another's finds.
Freeflag raiders use the place to refit and hide, which the Federation has noticed, and a navy visit here would not stop to ask questions.
A salvager at the bar claims to have found an intact hull in Gl 836.7 and will sell the coordinates to anyone who can pay in parts.
A brown dwarf, barely a star, with no world worth a dome, so nobody has ever lived here.
Its lanes to Deneb Algedi and Okafor make it a quiet back route for those who would rather not be logged.
A white dwarf, a burned-out cinder with hard radiation and a deep well, and no settlement has ever lasted here.
Pilots cross to Okafor and Deneb Algedi without lingering, and surveyors advise nobody to stay.
A red dwarf with nothing habitable, and nobody has ever tried to settle it.
It is a junction on the long way between Deneb Algedi, Placer and the Drift, and the lane to Gl 819A is used mostly by ships that do not want to be seen.
Prospectors staked claims here on the strength of the name, and the ore ran thin, so the claim markers are all that is left.
Nobody has lived here since, though salvagers say a few claim beacons still answer when pinged.
A red dwarf that flares, with no world a crew could hold, so nobody has stayed.
It sits between Wreckers, Placer and Gl 836.7, so ships pass through often and rarely stop.
A red dwarf with nothing worth settling, one short hop from Blind Eye.
Its lanes are used by Blind Eye crews who want a place to hide a cargo or wait out a patrol.
A red dwarf that nobody has ever settled, lying between Blind Eye and Gl 295.
Blind Eye crews use it as a hiding place, and surveyors say a few of their caches are still there, though not necessarily forgotten.
A red dwarf at the end of the line past Wreckers, with no world to live on.
Salvagers say hulks drift here, and the one lane out leads back through Wreckers or Gl 824.
The only lane out of emptied Corran ends at this dim red dwarf, and pickets have logged shades here since 2519, two years before Corran died.
Nothing has returned from the lane onward to Ascella, so what the shades do with the system remains unknown.
A pulsar sweeps hard radiation across this system on a fast, steady beat, and navy scans from 2519 onward show shade contacts moving inside it regardless.
It is a dead end with one lane, to Gl 654.3, and no one has gone in to see what the shades want here.
Jump arrivals here land inside the deep well of a black hole, a hazard that was keeping captains away long before shades were logged in 2519.
The lanes to 44 Ophiuchi and GJ 1217 are charted only from the edges, and nothing is known about the system itself.
Lying one lane past emptied Mallory, this white star was logged as shade territory from 2519, and navy charts treat it as the front door to Blightspace.
Pickets report contacts on the lane in both directions, but no ship has crossed to GJ 9600 and come back to say what lies between.
A black hole with three lanes, to HIP 86489, Mallory and HIP 81385, makes this the nearest thing Blightspace has to a crossroads, and shades have held it since 2519.
Navy analysts would love to know why a hazard star with such an awkward well is worth holding, and have no answer.
Shades have been logged at this swollen red giant since 2519, on a lane from Mallory that carried ore traffic once, before anything here was worth fearing.
Its lanes run on to Alnasl and HIP 87330, and nobody has seen what moves along them.
A small red dwarf on the lane between GJ 9577 and HIP 82621, it has been held by the Shadow since 2519 and is far from every friendly beacon.
Scans show only a faint, cold star and some traffic that does not answer hails.
The white dwarf here has three lanes, to GJ 9577, HIP 81827 and Gl 654.3, and pickets have logged shade contacts on all of them since 2519.
Whatever shades want with a dead star's cinder is not in any report, because nobody has got close enough to write one.
A brown dwarf gives almost no light here, so scans are poor, but they were enough to log shade contacts from 2519.
The lanes to GJ 3996 and GJ 9600 are the only ways in, and the navy does not use either.
Shades have held this white dwarf since 2519, on a lane chain that links HIP 83147 to the dead end at Sabik.
No survivor, picket crew or salvager has ever reported seeing anything that was built here, or anything that lives here.
Ascella is a white star two lanes past the Corran side of Blightspace, and navy long-range scans have shown shade contacts since 2519.
The lanes to GJ 4074 and HIP 90611 are both long, and no ship has tried either since the front moved.
At seventeen jumps from Sol, Sabik is a dead end at the far edge of Blightspace, with a single lane to HIP 82621 and shades logged since 2519.
Nobody has charted it beyond a star type and a distance, and the navy has no plan to learn more.
A red dwarf on the short lanes to GJ 1217 and Gl 650, held by the Shadow since 2519 and quiet on every scan the navy has managed.
The quiet has convinced no one, and no ship has gone in to test it.
This brown dwarf is a dead end with one lane, to GJ 3996, and pickets logged shade contacts here from 2519.
A system that hard to reach and that dim should hold nothing worth taking, so why the shades hold it is unknown.
Shades have held this red dwarf since 2519, and it sits on the short lane between HIP 81385 and HIP 83147.
Charts show no more than a star type and two lanes, and the navy has not sent a ship to add to them.
A pulsar dead end off HIP 81385, with radiation that scrambles scans, so the shade contacts logged since 2519 are the best the navy has.
Nobody can say whether the shades are here for the pulsar or in spite of it.
The lanes from this red dwarf run to Gl 695.1 and HIP 84425, and shades have been logged on both since 2519.
The navy has no recorded survey of the system, and no one who has been inside it.
A black hole whose well makes arrivals dangerous, held by the Shadow since 2519 and joined by lane to HIP 89620 and Ascella.
Scans show nothing in the system but the hole, which tells nobody anything useful.
Alnasl is a red giant with lanes to HIP 89620 and Gl 695.1, and the shades have held it since 2519.
The big star's glare blinds most long-range scans, so what the shades do here is not known.
Shade contacts at this white dwarf were first logged in 2519, on the short lanes between Alnasl and HIP 90611.
Pickets never came closer than a lane's length, and the system has gone unseen since.
The last red dwarf at the end of a single long lane from HIP 87330, held by the Shadow since 2519 and a hundred light years from Sol.
It is the farthest point of Blightspace on the navy's charts, and the charts stop there.
Bread was settled in 2357 as an ice stop for haulers working the outer ring's frozen debris, and grew into a town because water is always wanted somewhere.
With about six million people it is the largest settlement in the Cells, and its ice port and its haven port keep half the region's neighbours in water and in debt to it.
The haven is full, security is thin and unrest runs high: Bread is a Freeflag cell with no friendly territory behind it, and food and medicine arrive on sufferance.
Of its three lanes, the one through GJ 4355 toward the Margins is a choke point, and the only road out that nobody on either side bothers to watch.
Tarrow was settled in 2360 as a gas colony, skimming fuel for the haulers of the Rush, and stayed small and stubborn for a hundred and forty years.
In 2499 Prism repossessed its habitat for defaulted loans and the navy cleared it; two hundred people died when the hab was vented, and the rebellion dates from that year.
Today about eighty-five thousand people skim gas and shelter runaways, and no Federation ship is allowed to dock; security is almost nothing, and everyone on the surface knows a name from the list.
A captain could ask who signed the repossession order and where the loan ledgers went, since there are people in Tarrow who would pay well to find out.
Helvetios was settled in 2422, late in the Rush's long tail, by ice crews who wanted somewhere nobody had already claimed and found a yellow star nobody had wanted.
Its ice port sends water and volatiles to the other Cells, and its haven shelters about fifty-six thousand people who prefer not to be asked questions.
Unrest is among the highest in the region and the garrison is a few armed freighters, but nobody has yet come to test them.
Lode, a dead white dwarf, is only 1.3 days away, and ships that need to vanish for a week are said to vanish there.
Defiance was settled in 2386 as a remote outpost; its name is older than Freeflag by a century, a joke by a long-gone survey crew that stuck.
It has no industry, only a haven port and about six thousand people living on what other systems can spare and on the fees of ships needing a quiet berth.
Security is the lowest in the Cells, and the outpost is held only because nobody else wants to feed it.
A haven that takes in everyone keeps no records, so a captain looking for a missing crew or a stolen cargo could start on its docks.
Free Harbor was settled in 2401 as a gas town on the edge of the Rush's last push, and its name was meant as a boast about berthing fees.
About two million people live here, and its gas port supplies fuel to most of the Cells and to anyone who will pay in cargo rather than credit.
All three of its lanes run through dead red dwarfs, so ships arrive slowly and can be seen from a long way off.
Unrest is high and the haven is crowded, and the lane to GJ 1098 leads on to Footwall Reach, a dead system few have charted and fewer have explained.
GJ 3052 is a brown dwarf, too cold and dim to warm anything, and nobody ever filed a plan to settle it.
It sits on the lane between Tarrow and the Ironhull Outposts, which makes it a place where Freeflag crews and quiet Ironhull cousins can meet without a port's paperwork.
Lode is a white dwarf, a dead star's hard small light, and the prospectors who named it found nothing worth a second trip.
It is a short hop from Helvetios and Defiance, which is why unmarked ships sometimes sit there for days, reactors cold.
GJ 4355 has a yellow star and no settlement, and the survey reports give no reason why, which has never stopped spacers inventing several.
It is the lane from Bread to the Margins, and ships that cross it tend to be doing something they don't log.
Gl 322 is a flaring red dwarf with nothing worth settling, and its lane runs on to Tailings in the Anvil.
Freeflag's gas haulers from Free Harbor pass through it, and are the only regular traffic it has.
GJ 1098 is a red dwarf whose flares make long stays unwise, and nobody has built anything there that lasted.
Its lane to Footwall Reach is the only way beyond it, and the charts for that side are thin.
Gl 308.1 is another flare-prone red dwarf with no settlement, a stop on the way to Footwall Reach for crews who are not in a hurry.
Free Harbor lies 1.7 days off, and its watch crews know the dead system better than any chart does.
Farmers from the Procyon side took up this red dwarf's thin light in 2196, breeding crops for red-tinged days and settling on the one world that would hold a field.
Grain and packed produce flow through its container-port towards Procyon and the Inner Sphere, which is most of what GJ 3522 is known for.
It is quiet, well policed and prosperous, and the only grumbling is over navy requisitions pulling freighter crews off the Procyon run for the front.
A clerk at the container-port has noticed sealed crates logged out for Gl 285 that nobody there has ever signed for.
Settled in 2200, GJ 3622 was one of the dozen systems of the Rush's first generation, and it has kept the navy garrison it was given to guard the Wolf 359 approach.
Wheat and cattle feed, container loads and a heavy military port make it a staging post as much as a farm world.
With the navy lifting ships and crews for the front, unrest here is higher than the garrison likes, and the quiet is the kind that gets patrolled.
A quartermaster is rumoured to be selling ration lots off the books, and the buyers are not all Federation.
A yellow-sun world settled in 2190, GJ 1002 grew from farming compacts into a habitat-ringed giant of some two and a half billion people.
