Its container-port sorts a large share of the region's food into lane-sized loads, and half the district's dockhands know each other's families.
Next door lies dead Gl 908, and past that Low Tide, so Blackhull goods trickle in alongside the grain and the customs office knows it.
Someone in the habitat ring is selling clean manifests that pass inspection, and nobody agrees on whose clerk is doing the copying.
Gl 412A, settled in 2192, is the most populous world in the Concord region, ten billion people on farmland and habitat rings stacked around a yellow sun.
It is as rich as the inner ring gets, and a great deal of the food on Federation tables passes through its container-port.
Size is its problem: ration boards, hab allotments and queues of every kind have grown into a bureaucracy that moves slower than any navy convoy.
An audit of the habitat ring's ration boards was ordered quietly last year and has not been mentioned since, which has left a lot of nervous people.
Gl 380 was settled in 2180, four years after the Valhalla Result, and is one of the oldest colonies of the Rush, now home to nearly seven billion.
Its military port watches the lane to Gl 445, where Prism's border begins, and the navy inspects everything that crosses.
Security here is the weakest in the inner ring, and the navy resents Prism's precautionary recall of navigation cores, which has grounded ships it needs.
Associates in Prism grey cross from Gl 445 carrying sealed cases that customs is not permitted to open, and a customs officer wants someone to ask why.
Red-dwarf GJ 1005A was settled in 2211 by smallholders from GJ 1002, and has kept its farms small and its navy port busy.
Its military port guards the choke point to dead GJ 2005 in the Margins, which makes it the region's front door for anyone coming in from outside the law.
Calm and orderly, but the garrison keeps its guns manned, and patrol crews complain that the Margins send up more empty hulls than they should.
Ships have been coming out of GJ 2005 with their transponders silent and their holds light, and none of them stop to explain.
Settled in 2198 under an orange sun, Keid grew as a farm-and-habitat world with a trade in grain and finished goods.
Its container-port sits on the lane to Epsilon Eridani, so Keid's cargoes reach the Inner Sphere faster than most.
The place is wealthy and tightly policed, and the local grievance is a navy requisition that took two grain haulers and a freight captain with them.
A hab-ring cooperative has filed for a transport charter outside Federation inspection, and nobody knows who is backing it.
GJ 1116A was settled in 2214 as the second wave of Concord farms pushed outward, and it has grown to four billion.
Its container-port ships grain and processed food towards Luyten's Star and the Inner Sphere, and the habitats take most of the grain that stays.
Calm, wealthy and well guarded, it worries mainly about shipping: fewer hulls, longer waits, and rising prices in the habitat markets.
A freighter captain at the port claims to have refused a charter for a hold of unmarked navigation cores, and the cores were not on the recall list.
GJ 3379 was settled in 2202 beneath a steady yellow sun, and its three lanes make it a junction for the Concord farm district.
It is known for its habitat rings and for dock crews who can turn a convoy around in a shift.
Prosperous and well policed, though traffic-heavy, and the waiting yards are full of ships stuck behind navy requisition orders.
A dockside union is rumoured to be quietly hiding hulls from the requisition lists, and the navy has begun to suspect.
HIP 33226, a red-dwarf farm world settled in 2236, sits out on the thin side of the inner ring with a population of under half a billion.
It supplies Gl 268 and the habitat belt with food, and its small container-port is all that lets it export.
A quiet, orderly place, where the main worry is that the Gl 268 lane is the only one worth using and the navy is leaning on it.
A retired navy pilot runs a salvage tug out of the habitat and is asking questions about the lane to GJ 1111 that he should not.
HIP 83609 was settled in 2245 and grew around a shipyard that builds freighters and navy escorts under licence on a yellow sun's steady light.
It is known for its yards and its military port, and the lane to Gl 667A on the Long Watch makes it a staging point for the front.
Prism's core recall has stalled several hulls on the slips, and the navy wants them anyway; the yard's managers are caught between the two.
A shipwright says one of the recalled cores was swapped out for a blank before it left, and he is willing to say who signed for it.
Settled in 2232, Gl 285 is an orange-sun farm world whose habitats and container-port serve the quiet end of the inner ring.
It sells grain and goods along its short lanes to GJ 3454 and GJ 3522, and rarely makes the news.
Wealthy, secure and dull, with the odd grumble that the navy has taken more freighters than the harvest can spare.
A port inspector found a hull whose cargo register matched another ship's, plate for plate, and nobody has claimed either.
Gl 664 was settled in 2248 around an ageing red giant, on a world far enough out to catch a long, warm, red-tinged season.
It is known for hardy crops bred to the giant's light and for the shielding its habitats need against flare and radiation.
It is quiet and well guarded, but the shielding is costly to maintain and a shortage of replacement components is starting to bite.
An engineer at the habitat says the sun's flares have been shifting pattern, and has been told to stop saying so.
Gl 783A, a yellow-sun world settled in 2243, has grown to two billion on farmland, container yards and a navy garrison.
Its military port covers the lane to Gl 784 on the Long Watch, and the garrison is as much a part of the town as the harbour.
Security is tight and unrest low, but the navy has been leaning on it for ships and crews and the town has noticed.
A garrison officer has been sending requests for relief to a command that no longer seems to answer.
82 G. Eri was settled in 2205 and is known for its shipyard, which builds the region's grain freighters and has done so for three generations.
Habitat rings and farm belts share a yellow sun, and the people are proud of hulls that last.
It is prosperous and calm, though the Prism navigation-core recall has left several freighters half-finished on the slips.
A yard foreman has a ledger of cores installed before the recall, and what he says is in it would interest the navy.
Delta Pavonis was settled late for an inner-ring world, in 2270, as the lanes opened towards Pellucid and the Long Watch.
A yellow-sun farm world with a navy port and a container yard, it sends food to the Long Watch and takes fuel and components in return.
Quiet and rich, with the garrison stretched thin and the farmers wondering when the front will want their sons.
A freight captain hears odd traffic on the lane to Gamma Pavonis, ships going out loaded and coming back empty.
GJ 3323 is a small orange-sun world settled in 2234, with a few hundred million people on farms and habitat rings.
It lies on the lane between Keid and Tabit, and sells grain and goods to both.
It is calm and prosperous and neglected by the navy, which has thinned its patrols here for the front.
Two freighters called in with engine trouble last month and were gone before the port authority could inspect them.
Gl 268 was settled in 2263 as a navy-backed farm colony on an orange sun, and the garrison has stayed.
It is known for its military port, quiet habitat rings, and the lowest unrest in the region.
The calm is partly drill: the navy recruits hard, and families here have begun to count how many sons the front has taken.
A navy chaplain keeps a list of names that the official casualty roll does not.
Gl 223.2 was settled in 2258 on a red dwarf's dim light, and has grown into a modest farm world of under half a billion.
Habitat rings and a container-port move its grain and fruit to GJ 3379 and GJ 3323.
Secure, orderly and short of replacement parts, it is starting to feel the thinning of the shipping lanes.
A crop-breeder says a blight has shown up in the red-light wheat that is not on any list of known diseases.
Gl 408 was settled in 2207 around a red dwarf, one of the region's early small colonies, and still has fewer than four hundred million people.
It exports grain and manufactures through its container-port and takes pride in running its farms without any outside help.
It is secure and prosperous but short of crews, as the navy has requisitioned its best freighters.
A cooperative has bought a retired hauler and is quietly refitting it, and nobody is saying with what.
Xi Boötis was settled in 2230 and sits at the edge of the Concord region, with a lane across the border to GJ 3839 in the Anvil.
Its military port inspects Ironhull ore ships coming in, and its farms feed the miners going back.
The navy's inspections are the grievance: Ironhull crews arrive angry about Varrow and Hesk, and the inspectors' patience is thin.
An Ironhull captain wants passage for the families of Varrow's lost crew, and has been told no by every office in the system.
Pellucid, catalogued as Beta Hydri, was settled in 2272 as a middle-ring shipyard world, the last of the region's big yards to open.
It is known for its shipyard and its habitat rings, and it builds smaller freighters for the Long Watch and the outer ring.
Security is thinner here than in the inner ring, and the yards are short of cores since Prism's recall.
A yard supervisor has let it be known that a Freeflag buyer is offering to pay for hulls without cores.
Tabit was settled in 2271 and grew as a middle-ring farm and garrison world, now close to a billion people.
Its military port keeps an eye on the outer lanes, and its habitat rings house half the garrison's families.
Wealth and security are moderate, and the garrison has been drawn down to feed the front, leaving the farms to look after themselves.
A patrol that left for GJ 1065 never filed its return report, and the garrison has not mentioned it.
p Eridani was settled in 2225 and is a rich orange-sun world of two billion with a container-port, a military port and a long memory of border scares.
Its lane to dead HIP 12703 is a choke point, and everything coming through it is inspected twice.
Wealth is high but security is thin, and unrest has crept up with the shortage of ships; its dockhands are sharp-tongued.
A salvage crew claims there are hulls drifting in HIP 12703 with their navigation cores missing, and none of them is on a register.
Valparaiso, catalogued as Zeta Tucanae, was settled in 2274 and is the smallest of the middle-ring worlds, with barely a hundred million people.
Its farms and habitat serve a navy port that watches the lane to Gamma Pavonis and the Long Watch.
It is neither rich nor secure, and its people feel passed over when ships and supplies go to bigger worlds.
A garrison deserter is hiding in the habitat, and the story he tells about the Long Watch is not the navy's.
Sabine, catalogued as Chi-1 Orionis, was settled in 2223 and grew rich as a relay world, where messages and news from four lanes pass through its port.
It is known for its relay, its farms and its garrison, and its operators hear more than any other port in the region.
The relay has been strained since the quarantine: traffic from the middle ring has thinned, and the operators have been told what not to log.
A relay technician keeps a copy of the traffic logs from 2524, and the logs show a pattern that was not supposed to exist.
Garrison, catalogued as Gamma Leporis, took its name from the navy post that stood here in 2221; the post is long gone and the farms stayed.
It is known for grain and for its habitat rings, and its container-port sits on the lanes to Gl 185A and dead Gl 190.
It is reasonably wealthy and thinly guarded for a place named for a garrison, which the locals find funny, and the navy does not.
Ships have been turning back from Gl 190 with damaged hulls and no log, and the harbourmaster would like to know why.
Rana was settled in 2273 as a navy-backed farm colony on an orange sun, and has grown to nearly a billion people.
Its military port covers the lanes to GJ 1065 and HIP 18899, and its farms feed the garrisons along them.
It is calm, with security moderate and unrest low, but the garrison has been shrinking and the farmers have noticed.
A farmer's cooperative has been trading with someone in dead Gl 173, who pays in components that have no serial numbers.
Bellamy, catalogued as Kappa-1 Ceti, was settled in 2259 and has grown to over three billion on rich farmland and habitat rings.
It is known for its container-port and its lane to New Lagos in Lighthouse Run, where it trades food for the Run's salvage and gossip.
Wealth is high but security only moderate, and unrest is climbing as shipping shortages hit the markets.
A captain from New Lagos is offering good money for hulls that do not need inspection, and the offers are getting bolder.
Providence, catalogued as 10 Tauri, was settled in 2288 as a farm town in the outer ring, and has stayed a town of some forty-three million.
It grows food and ships it through a small container-port to GJ 3224 and the Concord worlds, and it is the end of the line.
Security is thin, unrest is the highest in the region, and since Tarrow in 2499 Freeflag has had sympathisers in the fields and on the docks.
A freighter captain says Freeflag agents have offered to buy the whole harvest at a better rate than the navy, and some farmers are listening.
Van Maanen's Star is a white dwarf, a cooling cinder with nothing to settle, and the Federation keeps only a picket here.
The lane to Low Tide in Blackspace makes it a choke point, and navy crews call it the back door that nobody bothered to lock.
Wolf 1061 is a small red dwarf with no world anyone could build on, and it is held by the Federation mostly because of where it sits.
The lane to Prism's Gl 643 passes through here, so a navy picket watches it and the associates pretend not to notice.
Gl 473A is a white dwarf, and nothing in the system could hold a colony, but its position, two jumps from Sol, keeps it on every navy chart.
A picket watches the lane to GJ 1156, where the unheld red giant makes the traffic nervous.
Gl 908 is a red dwarf with nothing worth settling, held by the Federation on paper and used by smugglers in practice.
Its lane to Low Tide in Blackspace makes it the quiet route for Blackhull cargo heading for GJ 1002.
GJ 1156 is a red giant, and its wind and flares are a real danger to ships that linger; nobody holds it and nobody lives there.
The lanes to dead Gar and GJ 3667 in the Anvil make it a place the careful avoid and the desperate use.
Gl 190 is a red dwarf with no settlement, though it is held by the Federation and sits on the Garrison side of the Concord lanes.
The lane to Nowhere Much in the Margins makes it a choke point, and ships that come through it are not always the ships that left.
GJ 3135 is a red dwarf with nothing to settle, held by the Federation as a lane marker between GJ 3193B and the dead systems beyond.
Its far lane to GJ 1028 is a choke point and a dead end, and the navy does not send many patrols down it.
HIP 12703 is a red dwarf with nothing settled, held by nobody, and it sits at a choke point beside p Eridani.
Lanes to Gl 118 in the Sink and HIP 13218 in the Margins make it a crossroads for salvagers and a place where hulls go missing.
GJ 1028 is a red dwarf at the edge of the settled lanes; nobody holds it and nobody lives there.
It connects only to GJ 3135 and Gl 46, both dead, and what passes through it is nobody's business but its own.
GJ 1083A is a white dwarf with no habitable world, held by the Federation as a picket on the way out from Sabine.
The lane to Gl 169 is a choke point, and the navy logs every ship that takes it.
Gl 228A is a brown dwarf, too cold and dim to hold a colony, held by the Federation and visited only by navy patrols.
Its lane to GJ 3356 in the Margins is a choke point, and the patrols come back with less to say than they should.
Gl 173 is a red dwarf with nothing settled, held by the Federation on paper and left to its own devices in practice.
The lane to Nowhere Much in the Margins makes it a choke point, and Rana's farmers know it is not quite empty.
Gl 169 is a red dwarf, unheld and unsettled, on the margin between the Concord lanes and the Margins.
Ships use it to slip across the border at a choke point beside GJ 1083A, and few ask what they carry.
GJ 3331A is a white dwarf with nothing to settle, held by the Federation as a lane marker on the road from Gl 190.
The lane to Nowhere Much in the Margins is short for a choke point, and smugglers have noticed.
GJ 3224 is a brown dwarf too cold to hold a colony, held by the Federation as the last marker before Providence.
The lane to Seam is a choke point, and with Freeflag active nearby the patrols here are thin and nervous.
Scrapheap, catalogued as GJ 1062, is a red dwarf named for what salvagers found in orbit: old hulls and discarded hardware, and nothing alive.
The lane to Bright Prospect in the Margins is a choke point, and the salvagers who work here are not always fussy about whose hulls they strip.
Seam, catalogued as Gl 112.1, is a white dwarf at the outer edge of the Concord lanes, unheld and uninhabited.
Its choke point on the lane from GJ 3224 is the last stop before dead GJ 3142, and ships that go beyond it are rarely logged again.
A pulsar sweeps the Metronome with hard radiation on a beat you can set a watch by. Nobody lives there, and the navy holds it anyway because it faces the Shadow.
The Federation keeps pickets here, and since Avesta emptied they have been the nearest thing to a wall between the front and Gl 629.3. Crews call the posting the tick.
Gl 629.3 is a red dwarf with nothing worth settling, and it was never anything but a waypoint on the lane between The Long Watch and The Metronome.
The Federation holds it for the lane alone. Any ship coming back from the front passes through here, which makes it a quiet place to hear what the pickets will not put in their reports.
Settled in 2354 under a pulsar's hard light, Avesta was a hard place to live that people lived in anyway until the Shadow emptied it in 2523.
The navy has charted the system from The Metronome but does not enter. Whatever happened to Avesta's people, nobody has yet reported what was left behind.
Mallory was settled in 2370 around a brown dwarf, a dim place that stayed on the charts mainly because four lanes met there. The Shadow emptied it in 2522.
With Mallory gone, the lanes to Gl 695.1, 44 Ophiuchi and Gl 654.3 in Blightspace lead straight to the front, and the people holding those systems know it.
Corran was settled in 2454 under an ageing red giant, and in 2521 it became the first system the Shadow was known to have emptied. Every living thing there died.
Its only lane runs to GJ 4074 in Blightspace. Anyone who wants to know what happened there has to go in that way, and nobody has yet reported coming back out with answers.
GJ 3790 is a flare-prone red dwarf one jump from human space; surveyors logged nothing worth a claim, and nobody has bothered to dispute that.
Its lanes run to both Diadem and Shoulder, so Freeflag crews are said to use it as a back door when the navy is watching the main routes.
GJ 3382 is a dim red dwarf with no settlement and no charted world worth a landing, and it sits one jump inside the Drift.
Salvagers say the lane toward HIP 27922 in the Far Lanterns is quieter than the charts suggest, and quiet is why some crews prefer it.
HIP 11439 is an empty red dwarf, kept on the charts mostly as a place to wait between the Drift and the Federation's Gl 100A.
Crews dodging inspection at Gl 100A are said to drop out here and sit dark for days, so a ship that appears unannounced is probably not on a legitimate run.
Gl 301A is a dead red dwarf with only two lanes, one deeper into the Drift and one to Dry Well in the Margins.
Dry Well's scavengers treat it as a back yard, stripping what earlier claimants left and telling no one what they find.
GJ 4249 is a red dwarf with nothing settled and nothing worth settling, one jump from Gl 841A in the Long Watch, where Federation lookouts log whatever comes through.
Since the front began moving inward, ships leaving the Drift by this lane get checked harder than they used to, and the crews resent it.
HIP 84195 is a white dwarf, a cold and faintly burning cinder whose surveyed planets, if any survived, give off only hard ultraviolet and a lot of debris.
Four lanes meet here, to GJ 3990, DR-0029, GJ 1208 and the Shoals, so ships pass through often and stop rarely, since the light is bad for hulls and tempers.
Aldebaran is a red giant that swelled past usefulness long before anyone arrived; its inner worlds are cinders, and the survey of 2300s found nothing worth a charter.
Ships still cross it because three short lanes meet here and a fourth runs on to Cobb in the Margins, and the giant's glare makes a poor place to be followed.
GJ 3505 is a brown dwarf with no real warmth and no worlds worth the fuel, so no charter company ever bid for it.
It sits between Petal's living world and the Blackhull haven at Blind Eye, which makes it a dark corner where hulls with no wish to be logged pass each other without a word.
Ross 687 is a flaring red dwarf whose bursts cook any hab shell left unshielded, and that is why nobody stayed after the first survey.
It is one short jump from the Garden's Seedbed, so surveyors treat it as a waiting room and keep their torches cold when the Bloom is seeding.
GJ 3409B is a white dwarf, a dead star's cooling ember, and what planets it had were stripped long ago; nobody has ever found a reason to settle it.
Five lanes meet here, one of them to Prism's Lumen, so the traffic is real and mostly quiet, and Prism has never said what rides in its holds.
GJ 1048 is a red dwarf with a few airless rocks, charted once and never claimed, and left on the lists mainly because the lanes through it are useful.
It lies a day and a half from Gl 100A in the Concord Worlds, and with the navy stretched thin by the Shadow, the patrols that once swept it come far less often.
Gl 154.1A is a brown dwarf at the end of a thin pair of lanes, with nothing to mine, nothing to harvest and nothing to see.
Its one road out of the region runs to Stope Reach in the Margins, and the few crews who use it say it is quiet, which in the Drift is worth noting.
Belt crews, the grandparents of the Ironhulls, settled Chara in 2280 around a yellow star and a good seam of ore, and built the first refinery before they built a proper street.
Mining and refining are all Chara is known for: ore comes in from the Anvil systems on the two nearest lanes, and ingots and slag go out, and the whole town smells of both.
About 54 million people now live there, and it has stayed comfortably off for a middle-ring town, with a navy picket that actually turns up when called.
Unrest simmers all the same: Chara's crews have heard what the quarantine hides about Varrow and Hesk, and the Federation's habit of requisitioning refitted haulers has not helped their mood.
A captain could pull on the refinery manifests, where a few ingot loads each month leave under a Compact seal and never reach a stated buyer.
Nobody lives at The Furnace because its Wolf-Rayet star, Gl 508A, scours everything near it with radiation and stellar wind, and no hull short of a purpose-built one lasts long in its glare.
Chara's miners named it for what it does to a ship's plating, and pilots cut through only when the lane saves more time than the shielding costs.
Adit is a brown dwarf, Gl 521, too dim to warm anything and too far out to be worth a claim, and surveyors found no world there worth the fuel.
It stays on the Compact's books as a waypoint between The Furnace and Skerry, where the odd salvager comes through and the odd smuggler, too, preferring a lane that nobody watches.
A survey crew charted Spore in 2378, two years after contact, and nearly lost a tender to a seeding it mistook for weather; the Accord's seeding rule is remembered with that scrape.
Pale fruiting towers rise from the world under the white star and release their spores in slow cycles, which surveyors time from orbit like tides.
The Accord lets crews orbit, scan and use marked landing fields, and nothing more: no weapons hot, no sample taken, not even a boot scraping.
Survey logs say the cycles have been running shorter since about 2521, and the Bloom will not discuss it; a captain could carry the logs to someone who wants them.
Marsh was among the first worlds charted, in 2376, when the survey ships that found the Bloom were still arguing over whether anything here was alive.
The orange sun lights a world of warm, shallow, living water, laced with floating mats that move in patterns charts struggle to hold still.
Humans may fly over and scan it, but nothing may be drawn from the water, and the old survey buoy sits well clear, as the Accord asks.
The lane to dead Gl 403 is quieter than it was; one early surveyor's journals mention a second lit world there, and nobody has checked.
Charted in 2395, Verdance was surveyed late because its lanes run only to dead systems, and ships had to cross uninhabited space to reach it.
Under its yellow sun the whole land seems one green mass, dense canopy broken by bare ring-shaped clearings that surveyors say are kept cleared.
The Accord forbids touching what grows, and crews here are told so twice, because Verdance looks so much like old Earth that people forget.
Both lanes lead to dead stars, so a captain here is a long way from help; a salvager's rumour of a wreck on the HIP 50636 lane is still open.
Rainhold was charted in 2377, one of the early survey stops, and it has been the main crossroads of the western Garden ever since.
Cloud under the white sun is constantly condensing and falling on a world of tall, fern-like growth, and surveyors work from orbit more often than not.
Under the Accord crews may land only where the Bloom has marked ground, and a hot weapon anywhere in the system ends a licence.
Spore, Burgeon and dead Gl 403 all meet here, so Rainhold sees whatever news there is; recently it sees less, and nobody knows who is holding it back.
Surveyors charted Bough in 1396's decade after the first sweep, in 2396, working outward from Mere along a lane they never expected to be useful.
The orange sun's world carries one vast branching growth that spans a whole continent, and surveyors have given up counting whether it is one thing or many.
Humans can scan and orbit freely; landing is restricted to marked ground, and nothing, not a leaf, may leave the system.
Its only other lane runs to dead GJ 3732B, and ships that make the crossing report the Bough lane buoy occasionally changing its beacon pattern, unprompted.
Arbor was charted in 2380, when the survey push reached Zosma and needed a safe waypoint on the way back toward Marsh.
Huge trunk-like structures stand across the yellow sun's world, many kilometres apart, linked by something surveyors call roots because they have no better word.
The Accord lets crews orbit, scan and land at marked fields; trade with the Bloom here means being handed things, never taking them.
Zosma lies a short step along the lane and borders the Hedge, so Arbor sees more human traffic than most; a captain could sell passage and keep quiet about it.
Bower was charted in 2385 by a crew who followed a lane out of dead Gl 330 and found a lit world at the end of it.
Its yellow sun lights a world of woven, arch-like growth that surveyors say resembles a half-built city, though nobody claims it is one.
Human crews may scan from orbit and land only on marked ground, and the Bloom has made it clear it watches how they behave.
Both its lanes lead to dead systems, which makes it a quiet corner; a surveyor's note about a recurring signal on the GJ 3553 lane has never been followed up.
Tilth was charted in 2398 late in the survey, with a crew working the lane from Pollen and not expecting much.
The yellow sun's world is patched with enormous bands of dark, turned-looking ground in which grow rows of fine, regular shoots that no human hand planted.
Crews may watch and scan, but the Accord's bar on taking anything that grows applies sharply here, since a handful of soil looks harmless and is not.
Tilth sits between Pollen and dead GJ 3582, and surveyors say the planted rows have moved since the last chart; someone could earn a living re-checking.
Quickening was charted in 2382, and the name stuck because the survey crew saw the surface change colour within days of arriving.
Under its white sun the world cycles quickly through blooms, flushes of growth that rise and collapse in weeks, and surveyors time their visits to them.
The Accord forbids anything hot near a living world, and crews here are reminded that a bloom is not a good reason to fire a thruster.
Lanes to Burgeon and Mere join it to the heart of the Garden; the cycle has sped up recently, and the survey office wants to know why.
Mere was charted in 2387, when survey ships working the Bough lane stopped over to check the charts and stayed a season.
The orange sun shines on a world mostly covered by still, dark water, with floating gardens that rise and sink in a slow rhythm.
Crews may orbit, scan and land at marked shorelines, but nothing may be taken from the water, however clear it looks.
Mere links Bough and Quickening, and survey crews have noted that the floating gardens are drifting toward one coast, as if heading somewhere.
Pollen was charted in 2388, and it is the Garden's door to the Anvil: the lane to Wrack, an Ironhull system, is two days and change.
Under the white sun the world sheds fine clouds of pollen into its own upper air, glittering and visible from orbit like a second atmosphere.
The Accord applies as strictly to Ironhull crews as to anyone, and a few have learned that a hauler's gun is no reason to relax it.
Ironhull haulers now pass through with Federation inspectors asking questions; a captain with discreet cargo of news, not goods, could do well here.
Burgeon was charted in 2381, and it became a junction because three lanes meet there, to Mossdeep, Quickening and Rainhold.
The orange sun's world is dense with growth in tiers, from low mats to canopy, and surveyors have found it hard to say where the ground begins.
Human crews may scan, orbit and land at marked fields; the Bloom has sometimes moved the markers without warning, and visitors are expected to notice.
Mossdeep leads on to the Hedge, so Burgeon feels the pressure of the front first; there is steady work for anyone willing to carry surveyors.
Loam was charted in 2389 under the catalogue name Tau-1 Hydrae, one of the few Garden stars that old Earth astronomers knew by name.
The yellow sun's world is covered in deep, dark, living soil in bands that shift slowly with the seasons, and surveyors work from stable orbits.
The Accord bars taking anything that grows, and Loam is where that rule is hardest to keep, since the ground itself is alive.
Lanes lead to dead GJ 3553 and Winze and to Root; salvagers say there is a derelict on the Winze lane, and nobody has confirmed it.
Zosma was charted in 2383 and sits next to the Hedge: a 1.1-day lane runs to Sporefall, among the shortest in the region.
The white sun lights a world of long ridges, covered in slow-growing crust and pierced by wide vents that exhale warm, moist air.
The Accord applies in full, and crews from the Hedge crossing in are checked at the buoy and reminded that no weapon is to be armed.
Since Shadowfall the Hedge side is nervous, and Zosma sees refugees' rumours before the news; a captain can trade in what is heard, not what is held.
Canopy was charted late, in 2406, after the survey crews found the lane from Root and had little reason to go on until a probe sent back images.
Under the orange sun the world is overgrown with a single continuous layer of growth high above the ground, which surveyors have never been able to map beneath.
Humans may scan and orbit; landing is limited to a few marked clearings, and the Bloom is strict about leaving them as found.
The lane to Seedbed leads toward the Far Lanterns, and survey logs suggest the canopy has been thinning near the edge, which nobody can explain.
Mossdeep was charted in 2384 and is the only red dwarf among the Garden's living worlds, so its light is dim and its colours are strange.
Dark, dense growth covers the world under the weak red sun, and surveyors report it seems to hold what little light there is.
The Accord applies as it does elsewhere; with two lanes into the Hedge, Mossdeep is where human crews most often arrive armed and must be told to stand down.
Tendril and Dewfall are both close, and in the Shadow's time Mossdeep's lanes are watched; a captain might carry warnings between the Hedge and the Bloom.
Root was charted in 2401, at the end of a long lane from Loam, and the survey crew found a world that was clearly older than its neighbours.
Under the white sun, thick ropes of growth run across the whole surface like a root system, with larger nodes at junctions visible from orbit.
Humans may scan and orbit and land on marked ground; the Accord's bar on taking anything that grows is read here very strictly.
Root joins Loam and Canopy, and surveyors say the nodes pulse in ways that look like signalling; a captain with decent instruments might map it.
Undergrowth was charted in 2402, after survey ships ran the lane from dead Gl 351.1 in the Hedge and found a living world past it.
The white sun lights a world of low, dense, shaded growth, and surveyors say the ground is almost never visible from orbit.
Crews may scan and orbit and land in marked places; the Bloom treats stray lights and engine burns near the surface as a breach, and says so.
With only one lane to a living world and one to the Hedge's dead stars, Undergrowth is isolated; a few salvagers claim to have seen movement at Gl 351.1.
Rhizome was charted in 2392 and is a crossroads: four lanes meet here, to Undergrowth, Seedbed, Petal in the Hedge and dead GJ 3553.
Under the white sun the world is knitted with pale, thread-like growth that spreads over the land and out into shallow seas.
The Accord applies to all who come, whichever side of the Hedge they started from, and the Bloom has stopped one Federation tender at the buoy until it stood down.
Petal is only 2.1 days away, so Rhizome sees Hedge traffic; with the front moving inward, a captain could find steady carriage here.
Seedbed was charted in 2403 and is the Garden's last stop before the Far Lanterns, with a lane to dead Ross 687 beyond.
Under the orange sun the world holds wide basins of pale, fine soil, from which new growth rises in ordered, repeated patterns.
Humans may scan and orbit and land only on marked ground, and the Accord's rule against burning a torch through a seeding is posted on the buoy.
Since Shadowfall the Bloom has watched this edge closely, and survey crews say the basins are being sown more often; someone should ask why.
Human surveyors charted Glade in 2397, twenty-one years after contact, and have logged it on a rolling schedule ever since, reachable only through Lichen or Tendril.
Under its yellow sun they describe broad grown terraces that shift slowly between visits, and sounds nobody has yet matched to anything like speech.
The Accord applies in full: weapons cold, nothing that grows leaves with you, and survey crews scrape their boot treads before returning to the ship.
Each pass of the dead-reckoning surveys finds the terraces rearranged a little more, and the old charts are quietly failing.
A 2397 survey log describes a ring structure that no later crew can find, and someone in the Garden would pay for a second look.
Lichen was charted in 2399, and the name comes from the first survey crew, who saw pale grown crusts spreading across every hard surface of its main world.
Lichen sits between Glade and Sporefall, so it sees more survey traffic than most Hedge worlds, and its Bloom hosts have apparently noticed.
Surveyors report the crusts retreating from their landing sites, which they take as courtesy, though a few suspect it is a polite way of asking them to leave.
The Accord bars sampling, so every lab on the Garden side lacks a single gram of Lichen crust, and several have offered a lot for one.
Sporefall was charted in 2390, in the uneasy years after contact, and the first survey crews reached it by the Zosma lane because no other lane yet existed.
Its red dwarf gives a dim, ruddy light, and surveyors report clouds of drifting spores that fog optics and lodge in every seal.
The Accord forbids burning a torch through a seeding, and Sporefall seeds often, so Zosma-bound captains check the Bloom's signals before leaving the lane.
Crews that have worked the Zosma lane since Shadowfall say the spore clouds have thickened, and that the Bloom has started turning back ships it once let through.
A salvager's rumour says a survey cutter from 2391 vanished near the red dwarf, and that something grown now sits where she was last seen.
Tendril was charted in 2391, and it is the Hedge's gate to Mossdeep in the Garden, which makes it a hub for survey traffic.
Surveyors report long grown lines running between the orange star's worlds, like cables, and they pulse in slow sequence that crews have learned to log but not to read.
Visitors keep weapons cold and take nothing, and the few captains who have tried to stay quiet and poach a cutting have been turned away at the next lane.
Tendril lies two lanes deep from Glade and sees few ships, so what the Bloom does here goes mostly unwatched, and the Bloom seems to know it.
Petal was charted in 2404, and its yellow sun makes it among the more livable-looking Hedge worlds, though no human may settle it.
Lanes run to Rhizome in the Garden and to GJ 3505, a dead star in the Far Lanterns, so survey crews pass through on the way somewhere else.
Surveyors describe vast grown blooms that open and close on a cycle of weeks, and the Accord says to keep the torch cold during every one.
Captains who have crossed from the dead Lantern star say the Bloom here watches the lane more closely than it did before Shadowfall.
A surveyor's note claims the blooms open facing the dead star at GJ 3505, which nobody has been able to explain.
Dewfall was charted in 2394 under an orange sun, named for the film of moisture that grown surfaces seem to shed every dawn.
It has three lanes: one to dead GJ 3643, one to Fen, and one to Mossdeep in the Garden, so it is a modest crossroads.
Surveyors report living towers rising in the morning damp and drooping by dusk, and they log them hourly because the Accord forbids anything more intrusive.
Nobody lives at Dewfall, but survey crews linger in its lanes, and a captain with a hold of cold-weather gear can find work there.
A crew from Mossdeep claims the towers have begun to lean towards dead GJ 3643, a star with nothing on the chart to explain why.
Thicket was charted in 2410, the last of the Hedge's survey worlds, and it lies thirteen jumps from Sol, at the far end of a long thin chain.
Its white star burns hot, and surveyors report a dense tangle of grown barbs and branches that makes the inner system hard to navigate.
Lanes lead to Frond and to dead GJ 3570, so visitors are usually surveyors, salvagers working the dead star, or somebody lost.
The Accord applies here as everywhere, and the tangle grows thick enough to foul a hull that gets too close, which the Bloom may regard as its own enforcement.
A salvager's tale holds that a hauler lost near GJ 3570 drifted into Thicket's tangle intact, and has not been seen since.
Fernlight was charted in 2408, and its two lanes both run to dead stars, GJ 2077 and GJ 3598, so no live system touches it.
Under the yellow sun surveyors report feathery grown fronds taller than a hab ring, bending in a wind no instrument can find.
Because it sits so far from anything inhabited, Fernlight gets the fewest visitors in the Hedge, and its Bloom hosts get the fewest warnings.
Weapons stay cold and nothing leaves with you, and a captain who breaks either rule here will have nobody to blame but the dead stars.
Fronds were seen bending toward GJ 3598 in 2519, the year the picket went silent, and a few spacers draw a conclusion from that.
Frond was charted in 2409 under an orange sun, and it sits one lane from Thicket and two from the dead stars GJ 3576 and GJ 3598.
Surveyors describe a grown canopy that covers whole continents and rises and falls in slow swells, like the chest of something asleep.
The Accord forbids touching it, so crews study it from orbit with long-range optics, and nobody has ever walked beneath it.
The Bloom seems to know when ships come, since the canopy lifts a day before each arrival, which some crews find welcoming and others find unnerving.
A survey tech from 2412 left a note saying the swells are slowing, and no later crew has agreed or disagreed.
Fen was charted in 2405 around a red dwarf, and three lanes meet here: two to dead stars, GJ 3624 and GJ 3598, and one to Dewfall.
Surveyors report waterlogged lowlands covered in grown reeds that glow faintly in the red light, and strings of floating growths that drift without a current.
Visitors must keep weapons cold and take nothing, and Fen's dim light makes the rule hard to police, which the Bloom may count on.
As the Shadow's front moves inward, captains in the Hedge have started to wonder whether Fen's quiet is peace or something being held back.
A rumour says the glowing reeds brightened for three days in 2521, the week Corran died, and a surveyor has the logs.
Mining crews settled Grist in 2314, during the Rush, bolting their first habitats to the rock under an orange sun and leaving the name of a grinding mill.
It is a working town of about twelve million, known for its ore and its refineries, and for sending ingots on to 85 Pegasi's forges.
Grist is comfortable by Compact standards, but the families of Varrow and Hesk crews drink here, and they say the Federation's silence makes them angrier than the Glass.
Grist sits cut off from the main Compact, with two dead lanes behind it, and its patrol hulls are thin on the ground and mostly old.
A captain could pick up work hauling refinery output on the long way round, where crews who dislike the Compact's route pay to ask no questions.
The Ironhulls settled 85 Pegasi in 2341, twenty-seven years after Grist, and built the yellow-star world into a forge-city of about 530 million.
Its mines feed its refineries, its refineries feed its forges, and its forges turn out hull plate, struts and, lately, gun mounts for refitted haulers.
The Federation wants those refitted ships and their crews for the Shadow front, and 85 Pegasi has started to resent how politely it is being asked.
Unrest is lower here than elsewhere in the Compact, but Freeflag handbills turn up in the forge districts and the foremen have stopped tearing them down.
A captain could find out who is quietly paying for the gun mounts that leave the forges without a Federation inspection stamp.
Gl 12 is a red dwarf with nothing worth settling, a dim, flaring star and bare rock, and nobody has ever filed a claim that held.
It matters only as a choke point: the lane from Grist and 85 Pegasi to the empty Cells passes through it, and salvagers and smugglers use that lane.
GJ 3061B is a red dwarf at the outer edge of the Outposts, uninhabited, and surveyors long ago wrote it off as not worth the fuel.
Its two lanes lead only to Grist and 85 Pegasi, so anyone sheltering there is either lost or has reason to stay out of sight.
Settled in 2212, early in the Rush, New Lagos grew from a few farm domes under an orange sun into a world of about 1.5 billion.
Its agri ports feed the neighbouring systems, its container port ships the surplus, and the navy keeps a base here to guard both.
It is rich and well guarded, with little open unrest, but ships and crews are requisitioned for the Shadow front, and dockers resent it.
A harbour clerk needs a sealed container carried to Barnacle unlogged; a captain could take the job and learn who in the navy office is paid to look away.
Barnacle was settled in 2266 as a small orange-star colony, and since the Charter Strikes it has been a haven for Blackhull crews with nowhere else to dock.
About 890 thousand people live here, running a container port that rehandles cargo no Federation yard would touch, and a haven that asks few questions.
Security is thin and unrest is rising: the navy sits across the choke point at New Lagos, and talk of the Glass cover-up and Freeflag works through the docks.
A captain could pick up sealed boxes bound for the inner ring, though the haven's wardens suspect a Federation informant is already working the quays.
Nobody lives at the Lighthouse: the pulsar sweeps the system with hard radiation, and no hull or habitat has yet been built to survive it for long.
The Federation holds it all the same, because four lanes meet here, and captains cross it fast, shielded and without stopping.
HIP 19255 is a brown dwarf with no light worth the name, and six lanes meet here, every one running to another dead system.
Salvagers treat it as a crossroads in the dark; the two nearest neighbours, DR-0008 and DR-0009, are known only by survey number, and few log a visit.
GJ 9120 is a red dwarf nobody settled, a dim, flare-prone star with nothing on the charts worth the fuel to stop for.
Its lane to Cobb in the Margins, three days out, makes it a quiet back door for independent traders who would rather not meet a navy inspection.
GJ 1052 is an ordinary orange star that nobody ever settled, and its charts have gone unrevised since the Rush ended.
It sits between the Federation's GJ 2030B in the Concord Worlds and DR-0014 in the Maw, so crews cutting across tend to travel with their transponders turned down.
GJ 1064A is a Wolf-Rayet star, and its radiation and stellar wind would strip an unshielded hull, which is the whole reason nobody lives here.
Outcrop Reach, three days down the far lane, is one of the few dead systems in the region with a proper name, which suggests someone once worked there.
GJ 3287 is a brown dwarf with no inner worlds worth mentioning, and no one has ever found a reason to stay.
Its far lane runs three days to Placer Reach, a name that suggests prospectors filed a claim there, and whether it ever paid is something no chart records.
GJ 3393 is an orange star with no settlement and no beacon, the kind of system the Rush passed through and never came back to.
A lane runs 2.7 days to GJ 3407B in the Margins, which makes it a handy dead-end shortcut for anyone who knows the other three lanes lead only to more emptiness.
Gl 581 was settled in 2238, in the first great rush outward, and has been a Federation world ever since, farmed under a dim red sun with mirrors and long patience.
About 240 million people live here, and the system is known for its grain, its stacked habitats and a container-port that handles much of the freight crossing the Concord Worlds.
It is rich, heavily garrisoned and calm, and the grumbling is about requisitions: the navy keeps taking freighters and crews for the Shadow front, and harvests wait on hulls that never return.
Its only neighbour in the Long Watch is dead GJ 3877, so the wider lane network runs through the Concord Worlds and the port supervisors know it.
A captain with spare hold space could be paid well, and quietly, to move boxes that the requisition lists conveniently forgot.
Gamma Pavonis was settled in 2269 as a breadbasket for the middle ring, and it still sells grain to mining systems that resent the Federation's prices and eat the grain anyway.
With about 1.6 billion people it is one of the biggest worlds in the region, all farmland, habitat towers and a container-port that never really sleeps.
Wealth is high and unrest low, but security is thinner than it looks, as the navy has pulled hulls towards the front and the Glass quarantine has made every nearby lane feel closer to trouble.
Under Prism's recall, nobody on the docks will say which navigation cores have been pulled, and a few haulers are flying on swapped units with no paperwork.
A captain could take a crate marked as recalled core stock from a quiet dockside broker, and would want to know where it is going before accepting.
Gl 644A is an orange star on the charts as a lane junction between Gl 664 and Wolf 1061, and nobody has ever found a reason to stay.
Navy traffic passes through on its way between the Concord Worlds, and the beacon here is maintained mostly because someone once wrote it into a schedule.
Gl 784 is a yellow star with nothing worth living on, and the Federation holds it only because the lanes to Gl 783A and Gl 754 pass through it.
Surveyors found no world that could hold a dome, which is the usual verdict in this region, and the system has been left to its beacon.
GJ 3877 is a brown dwarf, too cool to warm anything and too dim to light a dock, and its two lanes run only to Gl 555 and Gl 581.
Nobody lives here, though the lane to Gl 581 keeps a thin trickle of navy and freight moving through.
Gl 667A is a yellow star that looked good on early charts and gave nothing in the surveys, so nobody has ever put a roof over their head here.
It is a four-lane junction between the Concord Worlds and the Long Watch, and traffic that slows here is usually waiting on a navy inspection slot.
Gl 633 is a brown dwarf with no habitable rock and almost no light, and its lanes to Gl 667A and HIP 84051 are long and slow.
Crews call it a bad place to break down, since nobody is nearer than two and a half days and the navy rarely stops by.
Gl 842 is a red dwarf with no world worth the mass of a dome, and settlers who surveyed it went on to Gamma Pavonis instead.
Its lanes to Assay and Gamma Pavonis make it a quiet back-door, and the navy sometimes parks a picket here that nobody will admit to.
HIP 84051 is a red giant, swollen and unstable, and its radiation and deep well have kept every would-be settler away since the first survey.
Two lanes lead out to the Margins, at Long Shot and Cervantes, which makes it a choke point that smugglers and the navy both watch and neither admits to.
Gl 841A is an orange star in the outer ring, long surveyed and never settled, with nothing worth the cost of a dome.
Its lane to GJ 4249 runs into the dead Drift, and traffic here is mostly salvagers who go out and sometimes do not report back.
Gangue is a white dwarf, a cooling cinder whose radiation and well have kept it empty, and its catalogue name, Gl 676A, is the only thing that ever settled there.
Lanes run to Cervantes in the Margins and to Gl 629.3 in Corran Gate, so freight and rumour from Corran pass through on their way inward.
GJ 1251 is a red dwarf at the far end of the outer ring, and its use is as a gateway: from here a ship can enter the open Drift.
Nu Octantis, in the Outer Dark, lies three days off, and the Federation keeps GJ 1251 on its charts because nobody wants to lose sight of what is coming through.
Fomalhaut was settled in 2255 by prospectors working the second wave of the Rush, and it has been mining its rock and skimming its gas giant ever since.
Its three lanes lead only to dead systems, so the town's ore and fuel reach the Federation's Concord Worlds by way of the empty stretch at GJ 2005.
Roughly three million people live here, modestly well off and modestly guarded, with a tired suspicion of anyone who arrives asking about the quarantines.
A captain could find steady work running ore through GJ 2005 to the Concord choke point, and learn quickly which inspectors can be talked round.
Vasquez was claimed in 2308 by an ice-hauling cooperative whose charter-master gave the system his name, and it grew faster than any other Margins town.
With about 95 million people it is the Margins in miniature: its ice and gas ports feed everyone nearby, and it still can't grow enough food for itself.
Crowding, rationed water and a thin security presence keep tempers hot, and the meeting halls fill whenever a Federation requisition notice goes up.
A captain who can bring food, medicine or components in bulk will never be short of buyers, nor of people asking where the cargo came from.
Lindqvist was settled late, in 2433, by crews who had lost their berths in the long aftermath of the Charter Strikes and wanted somewhere nobody held a lien.
Its ice and gas ports keep about two million people alive, in a town that never quite grew past the first prefab rows.
Security is thin and tempers are uneasy, and the three dead systems around it make a quiet place for ships that would rather not be logged.
Salvagers here swear that wrecks lie unclaimed in the dead systems at Gl 851 and GJ 4201, and a few have paid to be proved wrong.
Quill was founded in 2306 by ice haulers who followed the first lanes out from Zeta Reticuli's cometary belt, two years before neighbouring Vasquez.
About three million people work its ice and gas ports, and it is the steadier of the pair: less crowded, less angry, and less noticed.
Its trade runs mostly to Vasquez, 2.3 days away, which gives it a market but also makes it hostage to any trouble there.
One lane leads to Gl 118, a dead system in the Sink, and ships have been seen coming back from it without papers.
Zeta Trianguli Australis was settled in 2335 by a mining syndicate that has long since dissolved and left its debts to the miners' children.
About two million people dig ore and skim gas, with a mining port that runs hard and a security force that barely runs at all.
Unrest is high for a town this size, mostly over pay, and the nearby lanes into dead systems make a good hiding place for anyone leaving owing money.
The 1.6-day lane to Long Shot carries most of its ore and most of its rumours, and a hauler willing to run it regularly will be known by everyone.
Long Shot was settled in 2323 under a white sun by people who bet their savings on a survey nobody else believed, and the name stuck.
The bet half paid off: its mining and ice ports support about three million people, none of them rich and all of them proud of it.
Its lane to HIP 84051 in the Long Watch is a Federation choke point, so every ore cargo goes out under navy inspection.
With the navy short of ships, inspectors have started eyeing local haulers as requisition stock, and a captain could be asked to carry what the owners would rather hide.
Capella was founded in 2346 under a dim red dwarf by a small crew of ice cutters, and it has never grown past a few thousand people.
Its single ice port is the whole economy, and with almost no security the outpost depends on whoever happens to be docked.
Unrest is high, and the lane to Gl 164 in the Ironhull Anvil means Compact crews and quieter visitors put in here and are not asked questions.
A captain could carry ice, news or a passenger across that choke point, if they can stomach not knowing which of the three it will turn out to be.
Nowhere Much was settled in 2316 by miners who named it as a joke, and the name stuck once the joke stopped being funny.
About two million people work its mining and ice ports, while all three lanes out run through Federation choke points into the Concord Worlds.
The navy inspects everything that leaves, and the town's anger at the delays feeds the sympathy for Freeflag that surfaces at its bars and notice-boards.
Smugglers say there is a quieter way past the Concord inspectors, and that the price of finding it is always more than the cargo is worth.
Bright Prospect was settled in 2342 by prospectors who followed a rich survey of the Tau-1 Eridani system belt, and the town is now about six million strong.
Its mining and ice ports keep the Margins' outer reaches supplied, but the system has almost no security and no authority above its own councils.
Unrest runs high, with miners' councils warning that the Federation's lane at Scrapheap will close on them the day the navy needs the ore.
A captain could take cargo to Dalim, 2.3 days away, or hire on with a council that needs guns more than it can say.
Dalim was settled in 2364 by families who left Bright Prospect when its claims filled up, and has stayed a colony of about 212 thousand ever since.
Its mining and ice ports sell mostly to Bright Prospect, and the two towns are close in the way of relatives who owe each other money.
With little security and rising unrest, Dalim lives with a constant fear of raiders, and the dead systems around it offer plenty of cover.
The dead system at Stope Reach, 2.5 days away, is named for old workings, and Dalim miners say those workings were never fully surveyed.
Dunmore was settled in 2332 by mining crews working the system's asteroid belt, and about 716 thousand people now live in the colony they built.
Its mining and ice ports ship out ore and water, while a lane to the dead system at GJ 3356 offers a hard 2.0-day run past a swollen red giant.
The navy rarely visits and security is thin, so the colony relies on its own defences and a long tradition of settling arguments in the back rooms.
A lane runs 2.7 days to Gl 233A in Prism Research, a dead system, and ships coming from that direction have had trouble explaining why.
Okafor was settled in 2326 by a mining crew led by the engineer whose name the colony carries, and about 437 thousand people now live under its yellow sun.
Its mining and ice ports supply ore and water to the outer Margins, and its closest lanes run into the dead systems of Blackspace.
Security is thin and unrest is climbing, and ships that dock with no transponder history are more common than the harbour office likes to admit.
A captain who knows how to run quietly could earn well here carrying cargo through Blackspace, though the people who hire for that rarely give their names.
Murphy's Claim began in 2367 as a single mining claim filed by a prospector named Murphy, whose deed has been disputed in the colony's courts ever since.
About fourteen thousand people work the one mining port, and every lane out leads to a dead system more than 2.6 days away.
Security is almost nonexistent, which suits some of the claim-holders and terrifies the rest, who worry about raiders and about each other.
A captain could carry a copy of the original deed to anyone who wants to buy the argument, or to anyone who wants it buried.
Ramsey was settled in 2350 by gas-skimming crews who found an ice-rich belt, and the town of about three million has quietly outgrown its welcome.
Its ice and gas ports sell fuel and water to every ship in range, and its position beside several dead lanes makes it a natural last stop.
Security is thin and unrest middling, with the town councils fearing both a Federation tax collector and a Freeflag recruiter, whichever arrives first.
The 2.7-day lane to Kittering is the only way the colony's goods reach a bigger market, so whoever guards it can name their terms.
Cervantes was settled in 2336 by miners who liked a quiet system, and it has grown into a town of about eight million that never stays quiet.
Its mining and ice ports are among the busiest in the Margins, and its lanes to Gangue and HIP 84051 open straight into Federation space.
The navy inspects, taxes and increasingly requisitions here, so security is the weakest it can be while the unrest is the loudest.
A captain could carry cargo out to Gangue in 1.4 days, or carry a crew out of the system before a requisition notice arrives.
Dry Well was settled in 2428 by a mining company that bet the system's name was a joke; it wasn't, and water is still brought in from outside.
About twenty-three thousand people hold on at one mining port, and the Drift lane to Gl 301A, three days out, is the nearest thing they have to a road.
Security is thin, unrest is high, and the place survives on spare parts and habit.
Salvagers come through from the Drift with stories of wrecks and abandoned ships, and the better-informed ones will pay for fuel and a quiet berth.
Pell's Folly was settled in 2412 by a speculator named Pell who sold shares in the system's gas and ice, and went unlamented when the shares failed.
About 43 thousand people stayed on and now work the ice and gas ports, supplying ships heading to or from the Anvil.
Security is thin and unrest is high, and the colony's debts, mostly held outside, have people nervous after what happened at Tarrow.
A lane to GJ 1092 leads on to Pollux in the Ironhull Anvil, and a captain with Compact friends can find work running that way.
Cobb was settled in 2368 as a single mining outpost, and about thirteen thousand people have stuck it out through every downturn since.
Its one mining port ships ore to anyone who will pay, and the three lanes out run toward the Long Dark and the Far Lanterns.
Security is thin, unrest is steady, and the outpost has learned to expect that strangers who ask about the far lanes are not here for the ore.
A captain could take the three-day lane to Aldebaran in the Far Lanterns, but nobody at Cobb will vouch for what comes back.
Nakamura was settled in 2343 by a mining crew from Iota Horologii's belt, and about 53 thousand people live in the colony today.
Its mining and ice ports sell mostly to Kittering, 2.0 days away, and the pair keep each other afloat through a trade that neither can afford to lose.
Unrest is among the highest in the Margins, with grievances over pay, debts and the loss of young people who leave to join Freeflag crews.
A captain could carry recruits or rumours between Nakamura and Kittering, and the lanes to the dead systems at Assay Reach and HIP 13218 are quieter still.
Hendry's Rest was settled in 2345 by mining crews who liked the name of their first strike, and about ten million people live there now.
Its mining and ice ports are large, its security small, and its unrest the highest of any big town in the Margins.
Anger here runs toward the Federation and Prism both, and Freeflag recruiters are not turned away at the door.
The lane to Drift Mouth Reach, 2.4 days away, leads toward the Drift, and a captain could find salvage, smugglers or trouble there, probably in that order.
Kittering was settled in 2352 by miners following ore finds in the Chi Eridani belt, and it has become a colony of about 773 thousand.
Its mining and ice ports make it a crossroads for Nakamura, Ramsey and the dark lane out to GJ 3102 in the Outer Dark.
Security is thin and unrest middling, and the colony prides itself on being the one place in the area that argues in committee before it shoots.
News from the far edge reaches Kittering first, and spacers here are quick to say what they have heard about the Shadow and slow to say who told them.
Grubstake was settled late, in 2448, by people who had nowhere else to go and a single ice port to go to.
About twenty-seven thousand people live in the outpost, and it is poor, short of everything, and very good at making do.
Unrest is high, security thin, and the two lanes into the Outer Dark are watched by people who have started sleeping badly.
A captain could supply Grubstake with food and parts and be treated as family, or ask about the Outer Dark and be shown the door.
Second Wind was settled in 2417 by survivors of a failed colony elsewhere, who named it for what they hoped to get and have not entirely got.
About twenty-one thousand people live around a single ice port, supplying water to passing ships from a system whose lanes all lead to dead neighbours.
Security is thin, unrest is high, and the colony is short of the medicine and components it cannot make for itself.
A captain could earn a lasting welcome by bringing medicine, or hear about the dead systems at Gl 912 and GJ 1284 from people who have prospected them.
Holloway was set up in 2443 as an outwatch, a listening post on the edge of the Outer Dark, and about two thousand people still keep it.
Its single gas port refuels the few ships that pass, and its crews trade fuel for news at every opportunity.
With almost no security and a view of the lanes into the dark, the watchers are jumpy, underpaid and aware that the Shadow has been moving inward.
The watchers keep logs of everything seen on the lanes toward GJ 3486 and GJ 3440, and a captain who brings supplies might be allowed to read them.
GJ 2005 has no world worth settling: bare rock and thin ice, which Fomalhaut's prospectors surveyed and left alone.
It survives as a waypoint on the lane between Fomalhaut and the Federation's Concord choke point, and as a good place to wait out an inspection.
GJ 3356 is a red giant, swollen and scorching, and whatever planets it once had have been burned bare or are too close to the radiation and the deep well to approach.
Nobody lives there, though Dunmore crews sometimes brave the 2.0-day run through it to reach the Federation choke point at Gl 228A.
GJ 1092 is a brown dwarf, too dim to warm anything, with a few frozen worlds and no reason for anyone to stay.
It matters only as a lane between Pell's Folly and Pollux in the Ironhull Anvil, and the haulers who use it do so without stopping.
Lucerne was settled in 2276, a yellow-star system six jumps from Sol, and by 2524 it was one of the two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring that went silent first.
Crews at Chi Draconis on the Anvil side say that nothing leaves the lane from Lucerne except ships in perfect formation, and none of them answer a hail.
Varrow was an Ironhull mining system, settled in 2311 and nine jumps from Sol, and it went glass in 2524 with its crews still aboard.
Its only lane runs to Calder, so the Federation pickets there are the only ones who see anything, and the families of Varrow's crews have been told nothing.
Facet, an orange-star system settled in 2300, was one of the first two Prism systems to fall in 2524, and survivors who reached Merrow described the lights changing colour all at once.
Its single lane ends at Merrow, where the Federation's quarantine is enforced and where captains still ask why Prism recalled certain navigation cores only after Facet went quiet.
Hesk was an Ironhull mining system, settled in 2339 and eleven jumps from Sol, and it went glass in 2524 along with Varrow.
Its only lane leads to GJ 4062, a Freeflag system, where recruiters use Hesk's lost crews to argue that neither the Federation nor Prism will tell the Ironhulls the truth.
GJ 1147 is a black hole, and nobody lives there because there is nothing to live on: no planet, no rock worth the fuel, only a well deep enough to ruin careless approaches.
Lanes run on to two more dead systems and to the Drift at GJ 3634, so a few captains cross it, giving the hole a wide berth and not lingering.
HIP 1031 is a red dwarf too dim and flare-prone to hold a colony, and the one survey that looked at it filed its report and went home.
Its lanes lead to three dead neighbours, one of them in the Drift, which makes it a quiet crossing for ships that would rather not be logged.
Gl 491A is a brown dwarf, barely a star, with no heat worth settling for and no planets anyone has bothered to chart in detail.
All three of its lanes run to dead systems in the Outer Dark, so it sits at the end of nowhere and is visited by almost nobody.
Nu Octantis is a red giant, swollen and unstable, its inner worlds long since scoured, so nobody settled here and the radiation off the star keeps lingering ships honest.
It is the best-connected dead system in this corner, with lanes to the Concord Worlds, the Long Watch and the Drift, so traffic passes through quickly and rumours sit here a while.
GJ 3486 is a white dwarf, a cooling cinder with nothing left to mine, and it was charted only because it lies on the way to the Margins.
Holloway and Grubstake are a few days off, and their crews use the lanes through here, so the odd hauler passes and the odd freighter with no flag at all.
GJ 3102 is a brown dwarf with no planets worth the name, and nobody has ever filed a claim on it, which in this region is nearly an achievement.
Its one settled neighbour is Kittering in the Margins, three days off, whose people sometimes drift out here for quiet, salvage or something they would rather not discuss.
Halcyon Dynamics settled GJ 1245A in 2256, building under lamps around a dim red dwarf that flares often enough to be written into every work contract.
Today about 442 million people run its forges, its research port and a relay that carries Prism traffic between the Inner Sphere and the rest of the region.
Unrest here is a little higher than in most Prism worlds, and relay staff mutter that the recall notices reached them before any explanation did.
A captain could hire on to haul spare relay parts and listen to what the operators say about the traffic they no longer pass on.
70 Ophiuchi was settled in 2250 by Halcyon, which put its first foundries on the warm side of an orange sun and its crews in orbital habitats.
About 911 million people now live here, working forges and research yards that turn out components for half the region's shipyards.
Everything is clean and well guarded, and the only grumbling is over housing allocations in the older habitats, which are assigned by an associate nobody has met.
Dockworkers say a backlog of recalled navigation cores is stacked in the research yards, and a captain who asks the wrong clerk might learn where they went.
Gl 873 was settled in 2239 around a plain yellow sun, and grew into the biggest world in the region, now home to about 4.3 billion people.
Its forges, relay and research port make it Prism's quiet engine room, and its lane to 61 Cygni carries Inner Sphere trade straight through.
Nothing is visibly wrong, which is the problem: a planet this crowded eats imported food and water, and any hiccup in the lanes shows on shelves within weeks.
Cargo masters here will pay well for dull, reliable freight, and a few of them are quietly stockpiling against the day the quarantine spreads.
Altair, a hot white star, was settled in 2251 by Halcyon, which wanted its light for research and built forges and habitats to feed on it.
About 493 million people live here, comfortable but less rich than their neighbours, and heavily patrolled by Prism security.
The white sun makes everything look new, and the habitat crews have learned to dim their windows and their opinions equally.
A captain could carry sealed research crates to Gl 752A and wonder why every manifest lists them as surplus.
Gl 445 was settled in 2227, early for a red dwarf, because its position three jumps from Sol made it the natural gate to everything beyond.
Today about 1.2 billion people live here, with forges, a relay and research port, and lanes to the Ironhull Anvil and the Federation's Concord Worlds.
Customs queues here are long and polite, and Ironhull crews pass through angry about Varrow and Hesk, which Prism's inspectors have learned not to mention.
A captain could carry a message between the Ironhull families asking after lost crews and the relay operators who may know more than they say.
Alsafi is the oldest world in the region, settled by Halcyon in 2209 under an orange sun, a few years after the first wave of jump colonies.
About 618 million people work its forges and habitats, and its research port holds the older Halcyon archives, which Prism neither shows nor throws away.
The old guard here remember when the company still had a human board, and they are careful to say so only among themselves.
A captain taking passengers to Alsafi might meet an archivist who wants something old carried out, and doesn't want to say what.
Gl 752A was settled in 2260, one of the later worlds in the region, when Halcyon filled the gaps between its older systems with forges and habitats.
About 1.4 billion people live under an orange sun, building alloys for the shipyards of Altair and 70 Ophiuchi next door.
Security is heavy and work is steady, but shifts have been lengthening since the recall and nobody is allowed to ask why the cores are late.
A captain willing to run short, unmarked lanes to Altair can make good money hauling parts that someone is in a hurry to forget.
Achird was settled in 2246 by Halcyon as a yellow-sun forge world, and its relay still carries more company traffic than any other in the region.
About 706 million people live here, and its lanes to Allure, Gl 892 and Groombridge 34 make it a hinge between the Prism core and the Inner Sphere.
It is wealthy, orderly and watched, and relay staff have been told to log every ship that has recently been near Allure or the Calder March.
A captain with a clean record might be hired to carry unlogged messages past the relay, for people who think the logs are being read.
Gl 625 was settled in 2262, Prism's furthest world from Sol in the region, and for a century was the quiet end of a quiet road.
About 2.4 billion people live here, working forges, habitats and research ports, and since 2524 their neighbour Lucerne has been Mirrorspace, a system gone glass.
Security is thinner here than anywhere else in the region, and Prism patrols watch the Lucerne lane while the Federation officially says nothing is there.
A captain could take evacuee stories and hard cash from people who want to leave, and learn what the quarantine is really keeping in.
Gl 892 was settled in 2220 and grew into one of the region's workhorse habitat worlds, with an orange sun, forges and big research halls.
About 1.7 billion people live here, and its three lanes to Achird, Gl 873 and Allure make it a crossroads for company freight.
Rents rise faster than wages in the habitats, and there are whispers of a work stoppage that nobody has yet dared to call one.
A captain could carry food to the habitat markets here and hear what the dockworkers will and won't do if the shortages come.
Gl 643 was settled in 2229 around a yellow sun, and has since become Prism's container hub on the border with the Federation and the Ironhulls.
About 458 million people work its forges, research port and sealed cargo yards, with lanes to Wolf 1061 and Quarle across two choke points.
Everything here is inspected twice, once by Prism and once by whoever is on the other side, and disputes over seals have closed berths for days.
A captain who knows how to read a manifest can make a living here, or lose one, depending on whose seal they trust.
Allure, catalogued as Mu Cassiopeiae, was settled in 2252 by Halcyon as a middle-ring forge and habitat world around a yellow sun.
About 2.6 billion people live here, and its lane to dead GJ 3126 is a choke point on the Ironhull border with Burr beyond.
Security is the weakest in the region, since Prism spreads its patrols thinly here, and locals have noticed which ships turn up and which do not.
A captain could take a quiet run to the GJ 3126 lane, where smugglers and Ironhull scouts are said to trade without much paperwork.
Vega was settled in 2278 as a company town of forges and labs under a white sun, and has never grown beyond about nine million people.
It is small, quiet and well off by outer-ring standards, with a lane to the Calder March that lets some freight slip past the bigger worlds' inspections.
Unrest is higher here than in most of the region, partly because the town is too small to hide anything from the company that employs everyone in it.
A captain might find Vega's forge crews willing to talk, and willing to pay, for news of what happened to the nearby systems.
GJ 3126 is a dead red dwarf, and nobody lives there; the charts agree on that and on little else.
Its lanes run to Allure and the Ironhull world of Burr, so it is a choke point both sides watch and neither admits to using.
Halcyon Dynamics settled Lumen in 2324 as a research-and-foundry world, long before the company became Prism, and the charter town has since grown into about 299 million people.
Its forges, relay stations and laboratories make it the richest world in the region, and what leaves its yards is mostly alloys and components that other Prism systems cannot make for themselves.
Security is thin for a world this valuable, and the quiet is uneasy: associates keep to company housing, and nobody on the docks talks about the recall notices for navigation cores.
Lumen is the region's door to the Drift via GJ 3420 and GJ 3413, and Prism sends survey crews out that way and does not publish what they find.
Alzirr is a company town of about 13 million, settled in 2363 as a relay and research post on the edge of the Drift.
Its relay stations carry most of the region's traffic, and the laboratories are small, clean and expensive. Almost everyone in town is on a Prism contract, and most know it.
Unrest is higher than the wealth would suggest, and talk of Freeflag in the outer ring comes in with every hauler crew, though nobody here has raised a flag.
Contract workers say a survey ship cleared for the dead lane to GJ 9231B went out last season and did not file a return, and the relay logs for it are missing.
Halcyon settled Candor in 2380, four years after Contact, and it has become the region's largest world at about 454 million, a place of forges, habitat rings and research campuses.
Its name is a polite cousin of CANTOR's, and the staff are tired of the joke; the research ports run mostly on work they are not allowed to describe.
Unrest is the highest in the region. The Glass has not touched Candor, but the silence about Varrow and Hesk has, and crews with Ironhull cousins are asking what the recalls were for.
A dock foreman on the habitat ring says the Prism associates are now doing their own cargo inspections, and one captain could find out why they stopped trusting the manifests.
Gl 233A is a red giant with a swollen, unstable star and no world worth settling, and its choke-point lane to Lumen is the only real way in from Dunmore.
Hauler crews cross it quickly, because the radiation off the star is hard on old shielding, and nobody stays long enough to wonder why the beacon is dark.
GJ 3398 is a dead yellow system that Prism holds as a waypoint between Alzirr and Candor, with no settled world and only an automated beacon to show it is claimed.
GJ 3420 is a red giant with nothing habitable, held by Prism as the quiet gateway between Lumen and the Long Dark, where its beacon outlasts most of the traffic.
Salvagers who have gone through it report empty survey stations and a lane marker nobody has maintained for years.
GJ 3413 is a dim red dwarf with no settled world, held by Prism as a staging point between Lumen and Alzirr and a gateway out to the Far Lanterns.
Survey crews report a few automated stations and a lot of debris, and nobody has yet agreed on whose it was.
GJ 3766 is a brown dwarf, too dim and cold to warm anything, and nobody ever filed a claim worth keeping. The charts list it as a waypoint and nothing more.
It sits one jump into the Drift, between Mattock's Ironhull miners and the uncharted dark, so crews dodging a navy inspection use it as a quiet back door.
GJ 3853 is a red dwarf with nothing to hold a settlement: no worlds worth building on, and a star whose flares make any hab expensive to shield.
It lies between two Freeflag systems, Remembrance and Strike, which makes it a handy meeting point for raiders, and a place where a Federation ship ought not to linger.
GJ 4189A is a blue giant, and the radiation near it would cook an unshielded hull within hours. Nobody has tried to live here, and the one hazard chart is thick with warnings.
Its lane to Wreckers makes it a Blackhull approach. A captain who can fly the long way round the star's worst flares will find the Blackhulls friendlier than the navy.
GJ 4329 is a red dwarf, flare-prone and barren, and nobody has found a reason to settle it. It is a stop on the road, not a destination.
One lane runs to GJ 4319, a Freeflag system in the Cells, so a trickle of supplies and fighters passes through. Whoever watches the lane knows who is arming.
Gl 765.4A is a red giant, swollen and unstable, its inner worlds scorched long ago. Survey crews wrote it off as soon as they saw the numbers.
It is buried in the Shoals, two lanes from anywhere that matters, so its few visitors are salvagers and the occasional ship that wants to be lost for a while.
GJ 3933 is a brown dwarf with no real worlds, only cold rock and dust, so there was never a case for building here. It stays on the charts as a junction.
Two Ironhull systems, GJ 3920 and Tarn, lie a lane away, and their haulers cut through here when the navy's fees seem high. Nobody there will admit it.
A black hole four jumps past the last human port, the Maw gave the region its name, and surveyors have never found anything there worth the risk of the approach.
The deep well is a real danger: salvagers who work the Drift treat it as a place to log, then leave, and the single lane to GJ 3174 is the only way back out.
DR-0014 is a white dwarf only two jumps into the Drift, uncharted beyond its lanes, with no recorded settlement and nothing to suggest anyone ever wanted one.
It is the region's crossroads, with four lanes running to the Long Dark and the Far Lanterns, so salvagers pass through often and stay only long enough to check their fuel.
Ice haulers and gas skimmers settled Tenpenny in 2327, late in the Rush, because a yellow star with plenty of volatiles was worth the awkward lanes.
Some million people now live in one sprawling town, and its two ports, ice and gas, keep the place alive and make it the last fuel stop for miles.
Every lane out leads to a dead system, so ships come in past the black hole or a dim red dwarf and leave the same way, and the docks are patrolled loosely.
No power recognises the town, and with the navy stretched thin by the Shadow and Freeflag, talk of requisitioned ships has people arguing over whether to hide their haulers.
Dock gossip says a gas-port captain needs a hauler willing to run the Sink lane without a navy transponder, and will pay in fuel and no questions.
HIP 31293 is a red dwarf with no world worth the cost of a habitat, and nobody has held a claim here long enough to leave a beacon.
It sits one short hop from Tenpenny, and the salvagers who pass through report only drifting hull scrap, most of it too old to trace.
Nobody lives at The Sink because it is a black hole: tidal stress and radiation from infalling matter make the well deadly to anything that lingers.
It is still the way into Tenpenny from Gl 118, and pilots time their transits carefully and pass the name along as a warning.
Gl 118 is a red dwarf with nothing settled on it, but it is a junction, with lanes running to Quill in the Margins and to the dead system HIP 12703.
Ships bound for Tenpenny wait here to check their fuel before committing to the black hole's lane, and the crews' wrecks and rubbish are the only sign anyone passes.
GJ 1077 is a brown dwarf with too little light or heat to support a colony, and the charts show no claim here worth the paperwork.
It lies at the far end of Tenpenny's longest lane, and the few surveyors and salvagers who have gone out report cold rock, debris and silence.
